lessons.title: Reading: Tolerance of the Rasoolullah (SAW)
lessons.notes_html:
Tolerance — The Central Quality

Tolerance means to bear pain or hardships with patience. It also means to bear things we do not like — for example, when we are in a position to take revenge but do not do so, we are displaying tolerance. The Rasoolullah (SAW) is the perfect model of tolerance.

Key Examples from His Life

  • Taif: The people of Taif threw stones at him, yet he did not curse them. Hazrat Jibrael (AS) said Allah had sent the Angel of the Mountains, who would let Al-Akh-Shabain (the two mountains) fall on them if the Rasoolullah (SAW) wished. He refused, hoping that Allah would let them beget children who would worship Allah Alone. He prayed for his enemies instead of taking revenge.
  • Conquest of Makkah: Abu Sufyan had been the worst enemy of Islam, yet the Rasoolullah (SAW) not only forgave him but honoured him by declaring amnesty for those who took refuge in his house. He declared a general amnesty and forgave all his enemies. Hazrat Ayesha (RA) said that he never took revenge upon anyone.
  • His servant: Hazrat Ans Bin Maalik (RA) said, 'I served the Rasoolullah (SAW) for 10 years. By Allah, he never objected to anything I said or did.'
  • Last address: He said, 'Revenge for bloodshed, as was the custom in the days of ignorance before Islam, is forbidden. I forgive those who murdered my cousin, Ibne-Rabiah.'

Word Meanings

  • revenge — deliberate punishment or injury inflicted in return for what one has suffered.
  • conquest — the act of taking control of a place by force; victory.
  • amnesty — a general pardon or forgiveness declared for offenders.
  • troubled — caused pain or worry to someone.
  • custom — a traditional and widely accepted way of behaving in a society.
  • forbidden — prohibited; not allowed.
  • objected — said something to express disapproval or disagreement.

To take revenge on one's enemies
To punish those who trouble us

mcqs.why: The people of Taif threw stones at the Rasoolullah (SAW) when he went there to preach Islam, yet he prayed for them instead of taking revenge.

mcqs.why: Hazrat Jibrael (AS) said that Allah had heard the people's reply and had sent the Angel of the Mountains to carry out whatever the Rasoolullah (SAW) ordered.

mcqs.why: He refused the offer and said he hoped Allah would let them beget children who would worship Allah Alone, praying for his enemies instead of taking revenge.

mcqs.why: Hazrat Ayesha (RA) said that the Rasoolullah (SAW) never took revenge upon anyone, which shows his perfect tolerance.

mcqs.why: Hazrat Ans Bin Maalik (RA) said, 'I served the Rasoolullah (SAW) for 10 years. By Allah, he never objected to anything I said or did.'

mcqs.why: In his last address he said, 'Revenge for bloodshed ... is forbidden. I forgive those who murdered my cousin, Ibne-Rabiah.'

lessons.title: Reading Skills: Fill in the Blanks, Main Idea and Topic Sentence
lessons.notes_html:
Fill in the Blanks — Answers

  • Tolerance means to bear pain or hardships with patience.
  • The Rasoolullah (SAW) is a model of tolerance.
  • Hazrat Ayesha (RA) said that the Rasoolullah (SAW) never took revenge upon anyone.
  • The Rasoolullah (SAW) went to Taif to preach Islam.
  • 'Revenge for bloodshed is forbidden.'

Main Idea

The main idea is the central point of a text. The main idea of this unit is that the Rasoolullah (SAW) is the perfect model of tolerance: he bore hardships with patience, never took revenge, forgave his worst enemies at Taif and at the conquest of Makkah, and prayed for those who troubled him. We, as Muslims, should follow his noble example, because the deterioration and conflict in society are due to a lack of tolerance.

Topic Sentence

A topic sentence states the main idea of a paragraph. The topic sentence of paragraph 1 is: 'Tolerance means to bear pain or hardships with patience.' It is the first sentence of the paragraph. The vivid verb in it is bear (to endure/carry); the specific words are pain, hardships and patience. The paragraph then extends the idea with another vivid verb phrase, take revenge.

mcqs.why: The solved exercise states that the Rasoolullah (SAW) went to Taif to preach Islam, where the people threw stones at him.

mcqs.why: The main idea is the central point of the whole text — here, that the Rasoolullah (SAW) is the perfect model of tolerance.

mcqs.why: The main-idea answer states clearly that the deterioration and conflict in society are due to a lack of tolerance.

mcqs.why: The solved answer points out 'bear' (to endure/carry) as the vivid verb; pain, hardships and patience are the specific nouns used in the sentence.

mcqs.why: The solved answer notes that after the topic sentence, the paragraph extends the idea with the vivid verb phrase 'take revenge' in the example sentence.

options: a minor detail of a paragraph
the main idea of a paragraph
mcqs.why: By definition, a topic sentence states the main idea that the rest of the paragraph explains or supports.

mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blanks exercise completes her saying as: he never took revenge upon anyone.

lessons.title: Vocabulary: Dictionary Skills, Syllables, Prefixes and Suffixes
lessons.notes_html:
Dictionary Table

  • declaring — /di-KLAIR-ing/, verb — announcing or stating something clearly and firmly.
  • preach — /preech/, verb — to deliver a religious speech; to teach or advise earnestly.
  • gracious — /GRAY-shus/, adjective — kind, courteous and pleasant.
  • deterioration — /di-teer-i-o-RAY-shun/, noun — the process of becoming worse.
  • conflict — /KON-flikt/, noun — a serious disagreement, struggle or fight.
  • menace — /MEN-us/, noun — a threat or a danger.

(Given example: refuge — ref-yooj, noun — protection from danger.)

Syllabic Division

A syllable is a word or part of a word that has only one vowel sound (e.g. amnesty — am-nes-ty).

  • helicopter: hel-i-cop-ter (4 syllables)
  • puppies: pup-pies (2)
  • market: mar-ket (2)
  • photographer: pho-tog-ra-pher (4)
  • patience: pa-tience (2)
  • excellent: ex-cel-lent (3)

Prefixes and Suffixes

A prefix is a set of letters added to the beginning of a word to make a new word; a suffix is a set of letters added to the ending of a word.

  • Prefix words: disagree, incorrect, impossible, redo, misunderstand, uninteresting, underwater, dishonest, rewrite, unhappy.
  • Suffix words: capable, terrible, beautiful, toothless, freedom, worker, payment, happiness, careful, kindness.

lessons.title: Writing: Paragraph Writing and Narrative Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Paragraph Writing (Model)

The model paragraph narrates a real-life incident of tolerance: during the break, a classmate accidentally spilled water on the writer's new notebook and all his homework was spoiled. At first the writer felt very angry and wanted to shout at him. But then he remembered the example of the Rasoolullah (SAW), who never took revenge on anyone. He controlled his anger, spoke calmly, and forgave the classmate when he said sorry. The classmate helped him copy the homework again, and they became good friends. The lesson: tolerance turns an enemy into a friend, while anger only spoils relations.

Narrative Writing (Model)

A narrative tells a story or incident in order. The model narrative is planned with a mind map: Title, Characters, Setting, Events, Conclusion.

  • Title: Tolerance of the Rasoolullah (SAW).
  • Characters: The Rasoolullah (SAW), Hazrat Jibrael (AS), the Angel of the Mountains, Abu Sufyan, Hazrat Ayesha (RA), Hazrat Ans Bin Maalik (RA).
  • Setting: Makkah Mukarramah and Taif, during the early preaching of Islam.
  • Event 1: At Taif he was stoned, yet he prayed for the people and refused the Angel of the Mountains' offer to crush them.
  • Event 2: At the conquest of Makkah he forgave all his enemies and declared amnesty, honouring even Abu Sufyan.
  • Event 3: In his last address he forbade revenge for bloodshed and forgave the murderer of his own cousin.
  • Conclusion: His whole life is a model of tolerance; we should follow his noble example to end conflict in society.

lessons.title: Reading: A Great Virtue
lessons.notes_html:
The Story in Brief

On a terrible stormy night, a hunter knocked first at the door of a poor old man's small hut in a forest. He had come to hunt, but because of the terrible storm and heavy rain he could neither hunt nor go back, so he asked for shelter for the night. One by one, a farmer and then a mother with her two small children also came. In all, six people were in the hut: the old man, the hunter, the farmer, a mother and her two small children.

Why the Old Man Refused No One

The old man did not refuse shelter to anyone because he was very kind and generous. He could not see people in trouble and was always ready to share with others whatever he had. He believed that if one has the will, one can manage, so he welcomed everyone who knocked at his door.

Why They Stood All Night

The hut was very small, with only one small bed on which only one person could sleep. With six people inside there was hardly room even to sit properly, so the whole crowd spent the stormy night standing in the little hut, chatting and praising the kindness of their host.

Lesson of the Story

We learn the great virtue of kindness and generosity. The old man was poor, thin and in rags, yet he shared his tiny hut, his bed and his milk with everyone. Sharing depends not on wealth but on the will: 'if one has the will one can manage.' Selfishness makes us feel guilty, as the farmer felt, while helping others brings respect and love.

Word Meanings

  • terrible — very bad or severe.
  • followed — came after.
  • hesitation — pausing because one is unsure.
  • step in — enter.
  • shelter — protection from danger or bad weather.
  • harsher — rougher and more severe.
  • accommodate — to provide room/space for someone.
  • generous — kind in giving and sharing.
  • shivering — shaking with cold or fear.
  • guilty — feeling sorry for doing wrong.
  • apologised — said sorry.

mcqs.q: Who knocked first at the door in the stormy night?
mcqs.why: The solved comprehension answer states that a hunter knocked first; he could neither hunt nor return because of the terrible storm and heavy rain.

mcqs.q: How many people were in the hut during that stormy night?
mcqs.why: Six people spent the night in the hut: the old man, the hunter, the farmer, a mother and her two small children.

mcqs.q: Why did the old man not refuse shelter to anyone?
options: He wanted payment from the guests
He was afraid of the storm
He was very kind and generous and could not see people in trouble
mcqs.why: The old man was kind and generous, always ready to share whatever he had; he believed that if one has the will, one can manage.

mcqs.q: Why did the people have to stand the whole night in the hut?
options: The hut was very small, with only one small bed for one person
They wanted to chat all night
The old man ordered them to stand
mcqs.why: With six people in the tiny hut and only one small bed, there was hardly room even to sit, so they stood all night, chatting and praising their host.

mcqs.q: What does 'shelter' mean?
options: Protection from danger or bad weather
mcqs.why: In the contextual meanings, shelter means protection from danger or bad weather — what the traveller asked for that night.

mcqs.q: 'Hesitation' means ______.
mcqs.why: Hesitation is pausing because one is unsure; the old man, without any hesitation, asked the traveller to step in.

mcqs.q: The great virtue taught by the story is ______.
mcqs.why: The story teaches the great virtue of kindness and generosity: the poor old man shared his tiny hut, bed and milk with everyone.

mcqs.q: According to the old man, sharing depends on ______.
mcqs.why: The story's message is that sharing depends not on wealth but on the will — 'if one has the will one can manage.'

mcqs.q: How did the farmer feel because of his selfishness?
mcqs.why: The solved answer explains that selfishness makes us feel guilty, as the farmer felt, and he apologised to the old man.

mcqs.q: 'Accommodate' means ______.
options: to provide room or space for someone
mcqs.why: The contextual meanings define accommodate as providing room/space for someone: the small hut could accommodate six people that night.

lessons.title: Reading: Story Study — Character Sketch, Elements and Dialogues
lessons.notes_html:
Book MCQs — Correct Options (from the story)

  • (i) The old man gave the hunter a cup of milk.
  • (ii) Only one person could sleep in the hut.
  • (iii) The second person to knock at the door was the farmer.
  • (iv) The farmer asked the old man not to open the door.

Character Sketch of the Old Man

  • Physical appearance: thin and lean, dressed in rags, living all alone in a small hut in a forest.
  • Personality traits: pious, very kind, noble and generous; he could not see people in trouble and was ready to share whatever he had, without any hesitation.
  • Accomplishment: On a terrible stormy night he gave shelter to five people in his tiny one-bed hut, gave them hot milk, set an example of a great virtue, and changed the selfish farmer's heart.

Elements of the Story

  • Setting: A small hut in a forest, on a stormy night of heavy rain.
  • Characters: The pious old man, the hunter, the farmer, the mother and her two children.
  • Event 1: The hunter knocks and is given shelter and a cup of hot milk.
  • Event 2: The farmer comes in and complains about the small hut.
  • Event 3: A mother with two children, shivering with cold, knocks; the farmer asks the old man not to open the door.
  • Climax: The old man opens the door and rebukes the farmer: 'Just imagine what might have happened if I had not allowed you in.'
  • Resolution: The farmer feels guilty and apologises; all six spend the night standing, praising the host's kindness.
  • Theme: Kindness and generosity — sharing what little we have with people in trouble.

Dialogues in the Story

Important dialogues: the hunter's request ('Sir, I am a hunter... I am looking for shelter'); the old man's answer ('if one has the will one can manage'); the farmer's selfish words ('How could we accommodate any more people?'); and the farmer's apology ('I am very sorry, Sir. I was selfish.'). Dialogues reveal the characters, carry the plot forward, create the conflict and its climax, and deliver the moral in the characters' own words.

mcqs.why: This is the book's own MCQ (i); the story elements confirm the hunter was given shelter and a cup of hot milk.

mcqs.why: Book MCQ (iv): when the mother and children knocked, the selfish farmer asked the old man not to open the door.

mcqs.why: In the resolution, the farmer feels guilty and apologises; all six spend the night standing in the hut, praising the host's kindness.

options: Kindness and generosity — sharing what little we have with people in trouble
mcqs.why: The theme stated in the elements is kindness and generosity — sharing what little we have with people in trouble.

options: They make the story longer only

mcqs.why: The solved answer explains that dialogues reveal the characters, carry the plot forward, create the conflict and climax, and deliver the moral in the characters' own words.

lessons.title: Vocabulary: Synonyms, Antonyms, Silent Letters, Diphthongs and Triphthongs
lessons.notes_html:
Synonyms and Antonyms

A thesaurus is a book that gives synonyms and sometimes antonyms of words. A synonym means exactly or nearly the same as another word; an antonym is opposite in meaning.

  • Synonyms: inferior — lower, poorer; respect — honour, regard; famine — starvation, hunger; profession — occupation, job; progress — development, advancement; bumper — abundant, plentiful; appreciated — valued, admired; perspired — sweated.
  • Antonyms: terrible — wonderful; hesitation — confidence; harsh — gentle; generous — selfish; cold — hot; pious — impious; night — day; step in — step out.
  • From the story: terrible (syn horrible; ant pleasant), kind (gentle; cruel), shelter (refuge; exposure), generous (charitable; selfish), guilty (ashamed; innocent), noble (honourable; base), stormy (wild; calm), trouble (difficulty; ease).

Silent Letters

Silent letters are written but not pronounced: know — silent K; knot — K; campaign — silent G; write — silent W; wrath — W; wrist — W; comb — silent B; wrong — W; knife — K; assign — G; reign — G; lamb — B.

Diphthongs

A diphthong is a sound formed by the combination of two vowels in a single syllable: train /ei/, eye /ai/, boy /oi/, oval /ou/, owl /au/, chair /ea/, ear /ia/, sure /ua/.

Triphthongs

A triphthong is a union of three vowel sounds pronounced in one syllable, as in fire: flower /aua/, tyre /aia/, player /eia/, lawyer /oia/, hour /aua/, quiet /aia/, fire /aia/, tower /aua/. In the given poem the triphthong words are: hour, shower, higher, fire, slower, power.

mcqs.q: A thesaurus is a book that gives ______ of words.
mcqs.why: The book explains that a thesaurus gives synonyms and sometimes antonyms of words; a synonym means nearly the same as another word.

mcqs.why: The thesaurus exercise gives famine — starvation, hunger, scarcity. Occupation is a synonym of profession, and honour of respect.

mcqs.why: The antonyms exercise gives generous — selfish, stingy, mean. Charitable is a synonym of generous, not an antonym.

mcqs.q: Which letter is silent in 'campaign'?
mcqs.why: The silent-letters exercise marks the G in campaign as silent; similarly assign and reign have a silent g.

mcqs.q: Which letter is silent in 'lamb'?
mcqs.why: Lamb has a silent B, like comb. The solved list also gives know, knot and knife a silent k.

mcqs.q: A diphthong is ______.
options: a sound formed by the combination of two vowels in a single syllable

mcqs.why: The book defines a diphthong as a sound formed by the combination of two vowels in a single syllable, e.g. /oi/ in boy.

mcqs.why: The antonyms exercise pairs step in (enter) with step out as its opposite.

lessons.title: Grammar: Plural Nouns, Countable and Uncountable Nouns, Punctuation
lessons.notes_html:
Plural Nouns

Rules from the book: add -s; add -es to nouns ending in o, s, ss, x, ch, sh; change y into ies; change f/fe into ves; some nouns change spellings (foot–feet, man–men, ox–oxen).

  • bench — benches; dish — dishes; bus — buses; box — boxes; quiz — quizzes.
  • candy — candies; family — families; berry — berries; city — cities; daisy — daisies.
  • From the story: man — men; child — children; night — nights; hut — huts; person — people.

Countable and Uncountable Nouns

Countable nouns can be counted; uncountable nouns cannot be counted (e.g. water, hair, milk, weather). In the exercise: milk — uncountable; eggs — countable; time — uncountable; nation, teacher, assignments, task, essay — countable.

Punctuation

Rules used in the telephone paragraph: a capital letter at the start of a sentence and for 'I'/proper names; a full stop at the end of declarative sentences; a comma to separate clauses; an apostrophe in contractions like 'That's'. Quotation marks are used to indicate direct speech, e.g. The hunter said, 'I am looking for shelter.'

mcqs.q: What is the plural of 'bench'?
mcqs.why: Nouns ending in -ch take -es, so bench becomes benches — like dish–dishes, bus–buses and box–boxes.

mcqs.q: What is the plural of 'candy'?
mcqs.why: For nouns ending in consonant + y, change y into ies: candy–candies, family–families, berry–berries, city–cities, daisy–daisies.

mcqs.q: Which noun changes its spelling completely in the plural?
mcqs.why: Some nouns change spellings in the plural: foot–feet, man–men, ox–oxen, child–children, person–people.

lessons.title: Writing: Good Deeds and Story Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Good Deeds for Daily Life

  • I can help someone to cross the road.
  • I can give my seat to an old person in the bus.
  • I can share my lunch with a classmate who has none.
  • I can help my mother in the kitchen.
  • I can teach a weak student his lesson.
  • I can give my old clothes and books to the poor.
  • I can water the plants and feed the birds.
  • I can keep my classroom and street clean.

Story Writing (Model) — 'Do good, have good'

Mind map: Characters — a poor woodcutter, a rich merchant; Setting — a village, a cold winter night; Problem — the merchant loses his way; Solution — the woodcutter shelters him; Theme — kindness is always rewarded.

Model story: On a terrible winter night, a rich merchant lost his way in the forest. Shivering with cold, he knocked at a poor woodcutter's small hut. Without any hesitation, the generous woodcutter gave him shelter, food and his own blanket, and himself slept on the floor. In the morning the merchant thanked him warmly. A month later, the woodcutter's daughter fell ill and he had no money for her treatment. The same merchant heard of it, paid for the treatment and gave the woodcutter work in his shop. The woodcutter's goodness returned to him. Moral: Do good, have good.

lessons.title: Oral: The Pied Piper of Hamelin
lessons.notes_html:
The Problem of Hamelin

There were too many rats in Hamelin. The people tried everything to get rid of them but in vain; even the cats could not do anything. The chief of Hamelin called a meeting and announced that he would give ten sacks of gold to anybody who saved them from the rats.

How Hamelin Was Freed

A stranger, the Pied Piper, took his pipe and played an odd but wonderful tune. All the rats ran after him through the streets to the river, where they fell into the water and drowned. Thus Hamelin was freed from rats.

The Broken Promise

When the problem was solved, the chief became greedy and did not want to pay the promised money. The Pied Piper was angry at this breach of promise and decided to teach him a lesson: he played his pipe again, and this time all the children of Hamelin ran after him to a cave outside the city, whose door he closed with a huge rock. Only when the chief and the people begged for forgiveness and promised twenty sacks of gold did he let the children go. The chief was ashamed of breaking his promise, and the people learnt never to break their promises.

Elements of the Story

  • Characters: The Pied Piper (stranger), the chief of Hamelin, the people and children of Hamelin.
  • Place: The town of Hamelin and the cave outside the city.
  • Time: A long time ago.
  • Beginning: Hamelin is full of rats; the chief promises ten sacks of gold to whoever removes them.
  • Middle: The Piper drowns the rats, but the greedy chief refuses to pay; in anger the Piper leads away all the children to a cave.
  • Ending: The ashamed chief begs forgiveness and offers twenty sacks of gold; the Piper frees the children.

A flood had come to the town

mcqs.why: The chief called a meeting and announced ten sacks of gold for anybody who saved them from the rats.

The cats killed all the rats
The rats left because of a flood
mcqs.why: The Pied Piper played an odd but wonderful tune; all the rats ran after him to the river, fell into the water and drowned.

mcqs.q: Why was the Pied Piper angry with the chief?
options: The chief did not thank him
The chief became greedy and refused to pay the promised money
The rats came back to the town
mcqs.why: When the problem was solved, the chief became greedy and broke his promise, which made the Piper angry.

mcqs.q: How did the Pied Piper teach the people a lesson?
options: He led all the children away to a cave outside the city
mcqs.why: He played his pipe again; all the children followed him to a cave, whose door he closed with a huge rock.

mcqs.q: How many sacks of gold did the people finally promise?
mcqs.why: Only when the chief and people begged forgiveness and promised twenty sacks of gold did the Piper let the children go.

mcqs.q: Why was the chief ashamed?
mcqs.why: The chief was ashamed of breaking his promise; he begged forgiveness and learnt never to break promises.

mcqs.q: Where did the Pied Piper take the children?
options: To a cave outside the city
mcqs.why: He took the children to a cave outside the city and closed its door with a huge rock.

mcqs.why: The elements exercise gives the time simply as 'a long time ago', the place as Hamelin and the cave, and the characters as the Piper, the chief, the people and the children.

mcqs.why: The ending states that the chief and the people begged forgiveness and learnt never to break their promises.

lessons.title: Reading: The Poem 'The Twins' — Comprehension and Figures of Speech
lessons.notes_html:
How the Twins Resembled

The twins resembled each other completely — in form and feature, face and limb, the poet grew so like his brother that nobody could tell one from the other. People (folks) took the poet for his brother and his brother for him — each for the other. Even their kith and kin (friends and relatives) were puzzled, and not a soul knew which twin was which.

How They Mixed Up

The twins mixed up one day in their infancy, before their names were fixed, while they were being washed by the nurse. By fate's decree — or rather the nurse's whim — the brother John was named as the poet, and the poet was named John.

At School

At school this fatal likeness dogged the poet's footsteps: he was always getting flogged (beaten) because his brother John turned out a fool and did foolish things, but the punishment fell on the poet, since no one could distinguish between the two.

The Poet's Question

In the last lines the poet asks everyone he knows: 'What would you do, if you were me, to prove that you were you?' He puts this question fruitlessly — nobody can answer it.

Rhyming Words

limb — him; brother — another; kin — twin; pitch — which; worse — nurse; fixed — mixed; decree — me; whim — him; school — fool; knew — you.

Figures of Speech

  • Alliteration (same letter/sound at the beginning of words): 'In form and feature, face and limb' — repetition of the f sound.
  • Hyperbole (extreme exaggeration): 'Yet not a soul knew which' — absolutely nobody could tell them apart; 'This fatal likeness even dogged my footsteps' — the likeness follows him like a curse.
  • Assonance (repetition of the same or similar vowel sounds in nearby words), in 'The Pied Piper': the repeated long 'e' in 'The chief became greedy...'; the 'a' sound in 'rats', 'and', 'began'.

mcqs.q: How did the twins resemble each other, according to the poem?
options: Completely — in form and feature, face and limb
mcqs.why: The poem says the twins resembled each other completely, in form and feature, face and limb, so nobody could tell one from the other.

mcqs.q: How did people take the twins?
options: Each for the other — the poet for his brother and his brother for him
mcqs.why: Folks took the poet for his brother and his brother for him; even their kith and kin were puzzled.

mcqs.q: When did the twins mix up?
options: On their first day at school
In their infancy, while being washed by the nurse, before their names were fixed
mcqs.why: The solved answer states they mixed up in infancy, during washing by the nurse, before their names were fixed — John was named as the poet and the poet as John.

mcqs.q: Why was the poet always flogged at school?
options: His brother John did foolish things, but no one could distinguish between the two
mcqs.why: This fatal likeness dogged him: John turned out a fool and did foolish things, but the punishment fell on the poet.

mcqs.q: What question does the poet ask in the last lines?
options: 'What would you do, if you were me, to prove that you were you?'
mcqs.why: The poet asks everyone this question fruitlessly — nobody can answer it.

mcqs.q: Which pair is a rhyming pair from the poem?
mcqs.why: The rhyming words listed from the poem include school — fool, limb — him, kin — twin, fixed — mixed, decree — me and knew — you.

mcqs.q: 'In form and feature, face and limb' is an example of ______.
mcqs.why: Alliteration is the repetition of the same letter/sound at the beginning of words — here the f sound in form, feature and face.

mcqs.q: 'Yet not a soul knew which' is an example of ______.
mcqs.why: Hyperbole is extreme exaggeration; 'not a soul' exaggerates that absolutely nobody could tell the twins apart.

mcqs.q: Assonance is ______.
options: the repetition of beginning consonant sounds
the repetition of the same or similar vowel sounds in nearby words
mcqs.why: Assonance is defined in the exercise as repetition of the same or similar vowel sounds in nearby words, e.g. the long 'e' in 'greedy' in the Pied Piper story.

mcqs.q: 'Kith and kin' means ______.
mcqs.why: The vocabulary matching gives kith and kin — relatives (friends and relatives), who were puzzled by the twins' likeness.

lessons.title: Vocabulary: Word Meanings and Simple Sentences
lessons.notes_html:
Matching — Words and Meanings

  • limb — a part of the body.
  • kith and kin — relatives (friends and relatives).
  • fearful — feeling or showing fear or anxiety.
  • fruitlessly — without results or success.

Lines Rewritten as Simple Sentences

  • 'That folks got taking me for him.' → People took me for my brother.
  • 'For one of us was born a twin.' → One of us was born a twin (we were twins).
  • 'We got completely mixed.' → We were completely mixed up (by the nurse).
  • 'This fatal likeness ever dogged.' → This unlucky likeness always followed/troubled me.
  • 'And I was always getting flogged.' → I was always beaten (punished).

mcqs.q: 'Limb' means ______.
mcqs.why: The matching exercise gives limb — a part of the body, as in the poem's 'face and limb'.

mcqs.q: 'Fearful' means ______.
options: feeling or showing fear or anxiety
mcqs.why: The matching exercise defines fearful as feeling or showing fear or anxiety.

mcqs.q: 'Fruitlessly' means ______.
mcqs.why: The poet asks his question fruitlessly — without results or success, because nobody can answer it.

mcqs.q: 'That folks got taking me for him' in a simple sentence is ______.
options: People took him for me always
People took me for my brother
mcqs.why: The solved rewriting gives: 'People took me for my brother.' — the poem's 'folks' are people and 'him' is the brother.

mcqs.q: 'We got completely mixed' becomes ______.
options: We were completely mixed up (by the nurse)
mcqs.why: The simple-sentence form given in the solved exercise is 'We were completely mixed up (by the nurse).'

mcqs.q: 'And I was always getting flogged' means ______.
mcqs.why: Flogged means beaten; the solved rewriting is 'I was always beaten (punished)' because John's foolish acts were punished on the poet.

mcqs.q: 'This fatal likeness ever dogged' in a simple sentence is ______.
options: This unlucky likeness always followed/troubled me
This likeness was fatal to the dog
mcqs.why: Dogged here means followed persistently; the solved form is 'This unlucky likeness always followed/troubled me.'

mcqs.q: 'For one of us was born a twin' simply means ______.
options: We were born in one day
A twin was born to us
One of us was born a twin (we were twins)
mcqs.why: The solved rewriting keeps the meaning in simple words: 'One of us was born a twin (we were twins).'

mcqs.q: Which word from the poem means 'relatives (friends and relatives)'?
mcqs.why: The matching exercise pairs kith and kin with relatives — even they were puzzled by the twins.

mcqs.q: A simple sentence should ______.
options: express the idea in clear, plain words
mcqs.why: The exercise rewrites the poem's lines in simple sentences — the same meaning in clear, plain words, e.g. 'People took me for my brother.'

lessons.title: Grammar: Pronouns
lessons.notes_html:
Choosing Pronouns (Fill in the Blanks)

  • It is unusually hot this year.
  • Where are the children? They were here a minute ago, but now I can't see them anywhere.
  • Amjad and I would like to go for a swim. Do you want to go with us?
  • Mrs. Malik brought her baby daughter to the picnic. She fed her yogurt and biscuits.
  • We have done our duty.

Reflexive Pronouns

Reflexive pronouns are used when the subject and the object of a verb are the same: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves.

  • He set himself a hard mission.
  • I was sitting by myself.
  • The girl choked herself.
  • You yourself can best explain.
  • The city itself is not very large.
  • They themselves admitted their mistake.

Pronoun–Antecedent Agreement

A pronoun must agree with its antecedent in gender and number: the stranger is singular and male, so he/his/him; the rats are plural, so them. Corrected: 'He said to the chief that he would get rid of rats. Then he took his pipe... All the rats in the town heard the music and began to run to him... The clever man took them all to the river.'

Indefinite Pronouns

Indefinite pronouns refer to a person or thing in a general way, not to anyone in particular. In 'The Pied Piper' they are: everything ('People tried everything'), anybody ('ten sacks of gold to anybody who saves them') and anything ('the cats could not do anything').

mcqs.q: ______ is unusually hot this year.
mcqs.why: Weather is referred to with the pronoun 'It': 'It is unusually hot this year.'

mcqs.q: Where are the children? ______ were here a minute ago, but now I can't see ______ anywhere.
mcqs.why: The children are plural: 'They were here a minute ago, but now I can't see them anywhere.'

mcqs.q: Amjad and I would like to go for a swim. Do ______ want to go with ______?
mcqs.why: 'Amjad and I' speak as 'us' (object), and the person addressed is 'you': 'Do you want to go with us?'

mcqs.q: Mrs. Malik brought her baby daughter to the picnic. ______ fed ______ yogurt and biscuits.
mcqs.why: Mrs. Malik is 'She' (subject) and her daughter is 'her' (object): 'She fed her yogurt and biscuits.'

mcqs.why: The possessive 'our' shows the speaker's group is the subject: 'We have done our duty.'

mcqs.why: The subject and object are the same person, so the reflexive pronoun 'himself' is used: 'He set himself a hard mission.'

mcqs.q: They ______ admitted their mistake.
mcqs.why: Here the reflexive pronoun themselves emphasises the subject 'They': 'They themselves admitted their mistake.'

mcqs.q: Reflexive pronouns are used when ______.
options: the verb is in the past tense
the subject and the object of a verb are the same
mcqs.why: The book defines reflexive pronouns as those used when the subject and object are the same: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves.

mcqs.q: A pronoun must agree with its antecedent in ______.
mcqs.why: The agreement exercise explains: the stranger is singular and male, so he/his/him; the rats are plural, so them.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an indefinite pronoun found in 'The Pied Piper'?
mcqs.why: The indefinite pronouns in the story are everything, anybody and anything — they refer to people or things in a general way, not to anyone in particular.

lessons.title: Grammar: Present Tenses
lessons.notes_html:
Simple Present and Present Continuous

Simple present: habits, general truths and facts — 'We go to school daily', 'The earth revolves around the sun'. Present continuous: actions happening at the time of speaking, temporary actions, and arranged near-future actions — 'My uncle is arriving tomorrow'.

Solved Examples

  • Mother is peeling potatoes in the kitchen at present. (action happening now — present continuous)
  • They lead a happy life. (habitual state — simple present)
  • My uncle owns this house, but I am living in it at present.
  • I do not wish to talk about this matter at present.
  • 'Is the gardener watering the plants?' asked my father.
  • Zara admires the poetry of Allama Muhammad Iqbal.
  • I understand what you are trying to tell me.
  • I usually go to school by bus but today I am going on foot.
  • I know what you think about.
  • The teacher advises the students to frame a time table for the holidays.

Paragraph 1 of 'The Pied Piper' in the Simple Present

'A long time ago, the people of Hamelin have a big problem. There are too many rats in Hamelin. People try everything to get rid of them but in vain. Even the cats cannot do anything. One day, the chief of the town calls a meeting. He tells them that he will give ten sacks of gold to anybody who saves them from rats.'

mcqs.q: Mother ______ potatoes in the kitchen at present.
mcqs.why: 'At present' shows an action happening now, so the present continuous 'is peeling' is correct.

mcqs.q: They ______ a happy life.
mcqs.why: A habitual state takes the simple present; with 'They' the verb is 'lead' — 'They lead a happy life.'

mcqs.q: My uncle ______ this house, but I ______ in it at present.
mcqs.why: Ownership is a state (simple present 'owns'), while living there at present is temporary (present continuous 'am living').

mcqs.q: I usually ______ to school by bus but today I ______ on foot.
mcqs.why: 'Usually' marks a habit (simple present 'go'); 'today' marks a temporary action now (present continuous 'am going').

mcqs.q: Zara ______ the poetry of Allama Muhammad Iqbal.
mcqs.why: A general fact/liking with a singular subject takes the simple present 'admires'.

mcqs.q: The simple present tense is used for ______.
mcqs.why: The book states: simple present is for habits, general truths and facts — 'We go to school daily', 'The earth revolves around the sun.'

mcqs.q: The present continuous is used for ______.
options: actions happening at the time of speaking and arranged near-future actions
mcqs.why: Present continuous covers actions happening now, temporary actions, and arranged near-future actions — 'My uncle is arriving tomorrow.'

mcqs.q: 'Is the gardener ______ the plants?' asked my father.
mcqs.why: The question is in the present continuous ('Is ... watering'), asking about an action happening at the time of speaking.

mcqs.q: I ______ what you ______ to tell me.
mcqs.why: 'Understand' is a state verb in the simple present; 'are trying' is an action in progress — 'I understand what you are trying to tell me.'

mcqs.q: In the simple-present rewrite of the Pied Piper paragraph, 'the chief of the town ______ a meeting'.
mcqs.why: The rewrite uses the simple present: 'One day, the chief of the town calls a meeting' — singular subject, so 'calls' with -s.

lessons.title: Writing: Paraphrase, Summary and Paragraph
lessons.notes_html:
Paraphrase of the First Stanza

'I grew up looking exactly like my brother in every way — in shape, in the features of my face and in every part of my body. We looked so alike that people started mistaking me for him and him for me. This confused all our friends and relatives very much, and the confusion reached a terrible height, because although one of us was a twin of the other, nobody at all could tell which of us was which.'

Summary of the Poem

In this humorous poem by Henry S. Leigh, the poet tells how he and his brother John were identical twins who looked exactly alike in form, feature, face and limb, so that everyone — even their kith and kin — mistook one for the other. As babies they were completely mixed up by the nurse before their names were fixed, so John was named as the poet and the poet as John. This fatal likeness followed the poet to school, where he was always flogged for the foolish acts of John. In the end he asks everyone, without success, what they would do, if they were in his place, to prove that they were themselves. The central idea is the funny confusion caused by the identical appearance of twins.

Model Paragraph — Daily Routine (Simple Present)

'I get up early in the morning. I offer my Fajr prayer and take a short walk. Then I take a bath, wear my uniform and eat breakfast. I go to school by bus and attend my classes carefully. I come back home at two o'clock, eat lunch and take some rest. In the afternoon I play cricket with my friends. In the evening I do my homework and revise my lessons. I eat dinner with my family, watch the news for a while and go to bed at ten o'clock.'

options: a shortened form of the whole text
the same text rewritten in your own words
mcqs.why: Paraphrasing restates a passage in your own words, keeping the full meaning — as the first stanza is restated in the solved exercise.

mcqs.q: Who is the poet of 'The Twins'?
mcqs.why: The summary names the poem as a humorous poem by Henry S. Leigh, about the poet and his brother John.

mcqs.q: What is the central idea of the poem?
options: The funny confusion caused by the identical appearance of twins
mcqs.why: The summary ends: the central idea is the funny confusion caused by the identical appearance of twins.

mcqs.why: A summary condenses the whole poem into its main points, while a paraphrase restates a part in full in one's own words.

mcqs.why: The summary says the babies were completely mixed up by the nurse before their names were fixed.

mcqs.q: According to the summary, the poet was flogged at school because ______.
options: his brother John did foolish things and no one could tell them apart
mcqs.why: This fatal likeness followed the poet to school, where he was always flogged for the foolish acts of John.

mcqs.why: The model paragraph uses the simple present for daily habits: 'I get up early... I go to school by bus...'

mcqs.q: In the model paragraph, the writer goes to bed at ______.
mcqs.why: The paragraph ends: 'I eat dinner with my family, watch the news for a while and go to bed at ten o'clock.' He comes home at two o'clock.

mcqs.q: In the model paragraph, what does the writer do in the afternoon?
mcqs.why: The paragraph says: 'In the afternoon I play cricket with my friends. In the evening I do my homework and revise my lessons.'

options: shape, the features of the face and every part of the body
mcqs.why: The paraphrase restates 'form and feature, face and limb' as looking exactly alike in shape, facial features and every part of the body.

chapters.title: Unit 4 — Let's Make Our Road Safer!

lessons.title: Talk Time and Oral Communication: Newspaper Reports and Speech
lessons.notes_html:
Features of a Newspaper Report

The report 'Youth killed in a road accident in Lahore' has these features: (1) Date of publication — 8 October, 2018. (2) Headline — 'Youth killed in a road accident in Lahore'. (3) Name of the reporter — ABC News reported. (4) City where the incident occurred — Lahore (Ichhra area). (5) Image with a caption — 'A youth was killed and another was wounded as their motorcycle hit a truck in Lahore's Ichra area.' (6) Structure: Beginning — introduction, what happened and how; Middle — eye-witnesses and other details; Ending — results of the incident, e.g. police help and casualties.

The Incident — Summary

In Lahore's Ichhra area, a youth was killed and another wounded when the motorcycle they were riding collided with a truck on Sunday night. Police and rescue teams reached the spot and shifted the dead and injured to hospital. Eye-witnesses and police sources said the accident occurred due to over-speeding by the motorcycle, so the youth riding it appears responsible, because over-speeding is the most crucial factor causing fatalities. Other reasons of accidents: using mobile phones while driving, not wearing seat belts or safety helmets, violating traffic signals, lane indiscipline and violating traffic signs. We can avoid them by observing traffic laws, driving within speed limits, wearing seat belts and helmets, never using a mobile phone while driving, obeying signals and lanes, and giving way to emergency vehicles.

Model Speech — Saving Lives by Following Traffic Rules

Research shows that almost 80% of traffic accidents take place due to the mistake or negligence of drivers, and most victims are young people below 30 years of age. If we drive within speed limits, wear seat belts and helmets, stop at red signals, keep lane discipline and never use mobile phones while driving, we can save precious lives. Violating a traffic law is an offence, and traffic discipline reflects the civility of a society.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a feature of a newspaper report?
mcqs.why: The features listed are: date of publication, headline, reporter's name, city of the incident, an image with a caption, and a beginning–middle–ending structure.

mcqs.q: In the report, the accident happened in which city?
mcqs.why: The report's city is Lahore, Ichhra area, where a youth was killed when a motorcycle hit a truck.

mcqs.q: According to eye-witnesses and police, the accident occurred due to ______.

mcqs.q: According to the model speech, about what percentage of traffic accidents happen due to the mistake or negligence of drivers?
mcqs.why: The speech says research shows almost 80% of traffic accidents take place due to the mistake or negligence of drivers.

mcqs.q: According to the speech, most accident victims are ______.

mcqs.why: The report's structure is: Beginning (what happened and how), Middle (eye-witnesses and details), Ending (results, police help and casualties).

a youth was killed and another wounded as their motorcycle hit a truck

lessons.title: Reading: Let's Make Our Road Safer!
lessons.notes_html:
Causes of Road Accidents

Five main causes: (1) over speeding and rash driving; (2) use of mobile phones while driving, which diverts the driver's attention; (3) not wearing seat belts; (4) not wearing safety helmets by motorcyclists; (5) violating traffic signals. (Also: violating lane discipline and traffic signs.)

How We Can Reduce Accidents

Recognise road safety as a social issue and discharge our responsibilities: observe traffic laws; drive within the given speed limits and reduce speed near schools, colleges, hospitals and urban areas; wear seat belts and helmets; avoid mobile phones while driving; obey signals, signs and lane discipline; and observe road courtesies — e.g. giving way to emergency vehicles.

Helmets Save Lives

Motorcyclists are highly vulnerable to fatal accidents. Wearing a helmet gives protection against severe head and face injuries, and so it increases the chances of survival by 80%.

Lanes

A road is divided into lanes through road markings (white lines); a lane is one of these sections of a wide road, meant to maintain traffic discipline. Keep in a particular lane and indicate properly (give a signal) before changing the lane. Lane straddling may cause a serious accident and invoke a fine. The extreme left lane is for heavy and slow-moving vehicles and the extreme right lane is for overtaking.

Emergency Vehicles

Whenever a driver hears the siren of an emergency vehicle (ambulance, fire brigade or police vehicle), he must give way to it, because the flashing red light means a life is at stake. Giving way lets it quickly reach the scene to help the ones in trouble.

Word Meanings

  • insecure — not secure or safe. congestions — the state of being crowded or blocked.
  • casualties — people injured or killed in an accident or war. offence — an illegal act.
  • penalise — to punish somebody for breaking a law or rule. negligence — lack of proper care and attention.
  • fatalities — deaths resulting from an accident. urban — relating to a city.
  • inclement — cold, rainy and bad (weather). invoke — to call for something; to bring into force.
  • penalties — punishments for breaking a law or rule. divert — to take attention away from something.
  • prohibited — forbidden by rules or laws. fatal — causing or ending in death.
  • vulnerable — that can be hurt or harmed easily. mandatory — required by law or rules.
  • violation — an act contrary to a rule. lanes — sections of a wide road. markings — a pattern of marks or lines. extreme — the farthest; very great in degree.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a main cause of road accidents?
options: Use of mobile phones while driving
mcqs.why: The five main causes include over speeding, mobile-phone use while driving, not wearing seat belts or helmets, and violating traffic signals.

mcqs.q: Wearing a helmet increases a motorcyclist's chances of survival by ______.
mcqs.why: The text states that a helmet protects against severe head and face injuries and increases the chances of survival by 80%.

mcqs.q: A lane is ______.

mcqs.why: A road is divided into lanes through road markings (white lines); a lane is one section of a wide road, meant to maintain traffic discipline.

mcqs.q: Before changing a lane, a driver should ______.
options: stop in the middle of the road
mcqs.why: The text says we should keep in a particular lane and indicate properly before changing the lane; lane straddling may cause an accident and invoke a fine.

mcqs.q: The extreme left lane is for ______.
mcqs.why: The extreme left lane is for heavy and slow-moving vehicles, and the extreme right lane is for overtaking.

mcqs.q: Why must we give way to emergency vehicles?
options: Because the law fines are high
Because a life is at stake and they must reach the scene quickly
mcqs.why: The flashing red light of an ambulance, fire brigade or police vehicle means a life is at stake; giving way lets it reach the scene quickly to help.

mcqs.q: 'Casualties' means ______.
options: people injured or killed in an accident or war
mcqs.why: The meanings exercise defines casualties as people injured or killed in an accident or war.

mcqs.q: 'Vulnerable' means ______.
options: that can be hurt or harmed easily
mcqs.why: Vulnerable means able to be hurt or harmed easily — motorcyclists are highly vulnerable to fatal accidents.

mcqs.q: Near schools, colleges and hospitals, drivers should ______.
mcqs.why: The text asks drivers to drive within speed limits and reduce speed near schools, colleges, hospitals and urban areas.

mcqs.q: Traffic rules regulate traffic by ______.
options: fixing speed limits, assigning lanes, and controlling crossings through signals and signs
mcqs.why: Traffic rules fix speed limits, assign lanes, control crossings through signals and signs, and punish violations so that road users move in an orderly and safe way.

lessons.title: Reading Skills and Vocabulary: Topic Sentence, Proofreading and Compound Words
lessons.notes_html:
Topic Sentence and Supporting Details

Topic sentence of paragraph 1: 'Every day when we go to schools, offices or markets we have to use roads and pass through traffic.' Supporting details: (1) Sometimes people violate traffic laws and this makes our roads insecure and unsafe. (2) The majority of victims of road accidents, unfortunately, are young people below 30 years of age. (3) Moreover, indiscipline on roads leads to traffic jams and congestions, which reflects negatively on us as a nation.

Proofreading — Corrected Passage on Over Speeding

'Over speeding is the most crucial factor causing fatalities or injuries in road accidents. Speed limits are specified for different roads. The drivers are required to drive their vehicles within given speed limits and should reduce speed near schools, colleges, hospitals, urban areas and during inclement weather conditions. Violations of prescribed speed limits not only endanger lives of road users but can also invoke penalties and legal action under traffic laws.' Corrections include: capital O at the start; 'in road accidents' (not 'rod'); 'drivers are' (not 'is'); 'drive' (not 'drove'); correct spellings of schools, colleges, hospitals, prescribed; 'endanger' (not 'endangers'); 'invoke' spelled correctly; full stops added.

Compound Words

A compound word is made up of two meaningful words and has a new meaning: alongside — along + side; grandmother — grand + mother; everything — every + thing; eye-catching — eye + catching; basketball — basket + ball; football — foot + ball; walkway — walk + way; sunflowers — sun + flowers; butterflies — butter + flies; upside — up + side.

mcqs.q: The topic sentence of paragraph 1 is about ______.
options: our daily use of roads and the traffic on them
mcqs.why: The topic sentence is 'Every day when we go to schools, offices or markets we have to use roads and pass through traffic.'

options: The extreme right lane is for overtaking
Indiscipline on roads leads to traffic jams and congestions
The report was published on 8 October
mcqs.why: The supporting details are: people violate traffic laws making roads insecure; most victims are below 30; indiscipline leads to jams and congestions.

options: reading a text carefully to find and correct mistakes
mcqs.why: The proofreading exercise corrects spelling ('rod' → 'road'), grammar ('drivers is' → 'drivers are') and punctuation in the passage.

mcqs.q: In the corrected passage, 'Over speeding is the most crucial factor causing ______.'
options: fatalities or injuries in road accidents
mcqs.why: The corrected passage begins: 'Over speeding is the most crucial factor causing fatalities or injuries in road accidents.'

mcqs.q: Which correction is made in the proofread passage?
mcqs.why: The listed corrections include 'drivers are' for 'drivers is', 'drive' for 'drove', and 'endanger' for 'endangers'.

mcqs.q: A compound word is ______.
options: a word with a silent letter
made up of two meaningful words and has a new meaning
mcqs.why: The book defines a compound word as one made of two meaningful words with a new meaning, e.g. basketball = basket + ball.

mcqs.q: 'Butterflies' is made of ______.
mcqs.why: The compound-words exercise breaks butterflies into butter + flies, sunflowers into sun + flowers, and walkway into walk + way.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a compound word?
mcqs.why: Eye-catching (eye + catching) is a compound word in the paragraph, along with alongside, grandmother, everything, basketball, football and walkway.

mcqs.q: 'Grandmother' breaks into ______.
mcqs.why: Grandmother = grand + mother, as broken down in the solved compound-words exercise.

mcqs.q: Violations of prescribed speed limits can invoke ______.

lessons.title: Grammar: Degrees of Adjectives, Articles, Apostrophes and Past Tenses
lessons.notes_html:
Degrees of Adjectives

Positive degree: no comparison. Comparative: compares two objects. Superlative: describes the highest quality of an object.

  • large — larger — largest; tiny — tinier — tiniest; cautious — more cautious — most cautious.
  • good — better — best; sad — sadder — saddest; young — younger — youngest.
  • helpful — more helpful — most helpful; comfortable — more comfortable — most comfortable.
  • friendly — friendlier — friendliest; wet — wetter — wettest; far — farther — farthest; bad — worse — worst.

Forming Adjectives

From nouns: friend — friendly; danger — dangerous; accident — accidental; brute — brutal; history — historical; person — personal. From verbs: obey — obedient; play — playful; talk — talkative; enjoy — enjoyable; help — helpful; read — readable.

Articles

'The' is used for a specific noun; 'a' before a consonant sound and 'an' before a vowel sound for a non-specific noun; sometimes no article is used. Solved: Sana put an orange in her plate. Javed bought (no article) chocolate milk. I ate the last piece of cake. An egg is shaped like an oval. The dog caught a stick. He likes to read (no article) short stories. We went on a field trip. The plates are on the dining table. My grandmother likes (no article) flowers very much. Their car does 150 miles an hour. I always listen to the radio. Is your mother working in an old office building?

Apostrophe — Contractions and Possession

Contractions: it is — it's; I am — I'm; you will — you'll; they will — they'll; you are — you're; we are — we're; they are — they're; is not — isn't; are not — aren't; cannot — can't. The apostrophe also shows possession: Ahmad's pen, the teacher's lounge, Sana's bag, my father's office; in plurals ending in 's' the apostrophe comes after the word — the boys' wooden homes.

Past Tenses

Simple past: an action completed in the past. Past continuous: an action going on at some time in the past. Solved: The room was full of guests when we arrived. He was sleeping soundly when I left the house. Asim got a new job three weeks ago. The gardener mowed the grass three days ago. Saqib came inside when the storm broke. The light went out when we were sitting for dinner.

mcqs.q: What is the comparative degree of 'good'?
mcqs.why: Good is irregular: good — better — best. 'Best' is the superlative degree.

mcqs.q: What is the superlative degree of 'bad'?
mcqs.why: Bad is irregular: bad — worse — worst. Worse is the comparative degree.

mcqs.q: Longer adjectives like 'cautious' form their comparative with ______.
mcqs.why: Cautious — more cautious — most cautious; likewise helpful and comfortable use more/most, while short adjectives take -er/-est.

mcqs.q: Which adjective is formed from the noun 'danger'?
mcqs.why: Adding suffixes forms adjectives: danger — dangerous, friend — friendly, accident — accidental, person — personal.

mcqs.q: Sana put ______ orange in her plate.
mcqs.why: 'Orange' begins with a vowel sound, so the article is 'an' for a non-specific noun.

mcqs.q: Their car does 150 miles ______ hour.
mcqs.why: We say 'an hour' because the h in hour is silent, so the word begins with a vowel sound.

mcqs.q: 'It is' contracts to ______.
mcqs.why: The apostrophe shows the missing letter: it is — it's; I am — I'm; cannot — can't; is not — isn't.

mcqs.q: In 'the boys' wooden homes', the apostrophe comes after 'boys' because ______.
mcqs.why: For possession in plurals ending in 's', the apostrophe comes after the word: the boys' homes — compare Ahmad's pen for a singular owner.

mcqs.q: He ______ soundly when I ______ the house.
mcqs.why: A longer action going on in the past (was sleeping, past continuous) is interrupted by a completed action (left, simple past).

mcqs.q: The comparative degree compares ______.
options: all objects for the highest quality
mcqs.why: The book defines: positive — no comparison; comparative — compares two objects; superlative — the highest quality of an object.

lessons.title: Writing: Paragraph, Accident Analysis and Newspaper Report
lessons.notes_html:
Model Paragraph — Pedestrians and Zebra Crossings

(Using the words mandatory, violation, penalise, fatal, vulnerable.) 'It should be mandatory for pedestrians to cross the road only at a zebra crossing. Pedestrians are the most vulnerable road users, and most fatal accidents happen when people cross the road carelessly from anywhere. Crossing away from the zebra crossing is a violation of traffic rules, and traffic police should penalise such careless pedestrians as they penalise drivers. Drivers, too, must stop before the zebra crossing and let people pass safely.'

Accident Analysis (Model)

Scene: On the Multan Road near our town, a speeding car hit a motorcycle carrying two students; traffic remained blocked for an hour. Causes: The car driver was over speeding and using his mobile phone; the motorcyclists were not wearing helmets. Injuries: One student received a severe head injury and the other broke his leg. Treatment: Rescue teams shifted both to hospital; the head-injured student was kept in the ICU. Remedies: Keep within speed limits; never use mobile phones while driving; motorcyclists must wear helmets; traffic police should strictly penalise violations; awareness campaigns in schools and colleges.

Newspaper Report (Model)

A newspaper report is written in the past tense with a headline, date and reporter's name. Model: THE SCHOOL TIMES — Date: 10 November. HEADLINE: 'Clean and Green Day Celebrated at Our School' — Reporter: Ali Raza. REPORT: Lahore — A 'Clean and Green Day' was celebrated at our school yesterday. Students planted two hundred saplings in the school ground and cleaned the classrooms and playground. The headmaster inaugurated the drive by planting a neem tree and advised the students to take care of the plants regularly.

mcqs.q: In the model paragraph, pedestrians should cross the road only at ______.
mcqs.why: The paragraph says it should be mandatory for pedestrians to cross only at a zebra crossing, since pedestrians are the most vulnerable road users.

mcqs.q: In the model accident analysis, the causes of the accident were ______.
options: over speeding, mobile-phone use, and no helmets
mcqs.why: The analysis lists: the car driver was over speeding and using his mobile phone; the motorcyclists were not wearing helmets.

mcqs.q: In the model analysis, what injuries did the students receive?
options: One had a severe head injury and the other broke his leg
mcqs.why: The model states one student received a severe head injury (kept in the ICU) and the other broke his leg.

mcqs.q: The head-injured student was kept in ______.
mcqs.why: Rescue teams shifted both students to hospital, where the head-injured student was kept in the ICU.

mcqs.q: A newspaper report is written in ______.
options: the past tense, with a headline, date and reporter's name
mcqs.why: The model report has a headline, date (10 November) and reporter's name (Ali Raza), and reports the event in the past tense.

mcqs.q: In the model report, how many saplings did the students plant?
mcqs.why: The report says students planted two hundred saplings in the school ground on Clean and Green Day.

mcqs.q: Who inaugurated the Clean and Green Day drive?
options: The headmaster, by planting a neem tree
mcqs.why: The headmaster inaugurated the drive by planting a neem tree and advised students to care for the plants regularly.

mcqs.q: An accident analysis is organised with a mind map of ______.
options: scene, causes, injuries, treatment and remedies
mcqs.why: The analysis mind map has five heads: scene, causes, injuries, treatment, remedies/suggestions.

mcqs.q: Which remedy is suggested in the model analysis?
options: Awareness campaigns in schools and colleges
mcqs.why: The remedies include speed limits, no mobile phones, helmets, strict penalties by traffic police, and awareness campaigns in schools and colleges.

mcqs.q: In the model paragraph, careless pedestrians who cross away from the zebra crossing should be ______.
mcqs.why: The paragraph says crossing away from the zebra crossing is a violation, and traffic police should penalise such pedestrians as they penalise drivers.

lessons.title: Oral: Poem 'Water' and Benefits of Traffic Rules
lessons.notes_html:
Poem 'Water' — Oral Answers

  • Water is brown and cool in a puddle: 'In a puddle brown and cool.'
  • A dewdrop is a tiny drop of water (dew) that shines on grass and leaves in the early morning; in the poem it is 'crystal bright' — clear and shining like crystal.
  • The rainbow has seven colours: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red. In a rainbow, 'far unfurled', there is 'every colour in the world'.

Main Idea of the Poem

Water is the loveliest thing in the world. It appears everywhere and in many forms and colours — dark and ripply in a spring, black and quiet in a pool, brown in a puddle, blue in a river, silver-grey in a raindrop, flashing white in a fountain, crystal bright in a dewdrop, frosty-cold in a pitcher, pink and gold in a bubble, and green in the summer sea — all the year, from spring to spring.

Benefits of Traffic Rules

Traffic rules keep our roads safe and save precious lives. Speed limits reduce fatal accidents; seat belts reduce the risk of fatal injuries by 50–60%; helmets increase a motorcyclist's chances of survival by 80%. Signals, signs and lane discipline keep traffic moving in an orderly way and prevent jams and congestions. Obeying traffic rules also improves our country's image and proves us a law-abiding, civilised nation.

mcqs.q: In the poem 'Water', water is brown and cool ______.
mcqs.why: The oral answer quotes the poem: 'In a puddle brown and cool.'

mcqs.q: A dewdrop is ______.
options: a tiny drop of dew that shines on grass and leaves in the early morning
mcqs.why: A dewdrop is a tiny drop of water (dew) shining on grass and leaves early in the morning; the poem calls it 'crystal bright'.

mcqs.q: How many colours are there in a rainbow?
mcqs.why: The rainbow has seven colours: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red.

mcqs.q: In the poem, water in a river is ______.
mcqs.why: The main-idea answer lists: blue in a river, brown in a puddle, silver-grey in a raindrop, pink and gold in a bubble, green in the summer sea.

mcqs.q: What is the main idea of the poem 'Water'?
options: Water is the loveliest thing in the world, appearing everywhere in many forms and colours
mcqs.why: The main idea is that water is the loveliest thing in the world, found everywhere in many forms and colours, from spring to spring.

mcqs.q: Seat belts reduce the risk of fatal injuries by ______.
mcqs.why: The traffic-rules answer states seat belts reduce the risk of fatal injuries by 50–60%, while helmets raise survival chances by 80%.

mcqs.q: In the poem, water is 'crystal bright' in ______.
mcqs.why: The poem's forms: crystal bright in a dewdrop, frosty-cold in a pitcher, black and quiet in a pool, flashing white in a fountain.

mcqs.q: Obeying traffic rules proves us ______.
mcqs.why: The answer concludes that obeying traffic rules improves our country's image and proves us a law-abiding, civilised nation.

mcqs.q: Water is 'frosty-cold' in ______.
mcqs.why: From the main-idea list: frosty-cold in a pitcher, pink and gold in a bubble, flashing white in a fountain, green in the summer sea.

mcqs.q: Signals, signs and lane discipline help to ______.
options: keep traffic moving in an orderly way and prevent jams and congestions
mcqs.why: They keep traffic moving in an orderly way and prevent jams and congestions, as stated in the benefits of traffic rules.

lessons.title: Reading: Review Questions and the Edhi Passage
lessons.notes_html:
Review Questions — Answers

  • Tolerance: At the conquest of Makkah Mukarramah, the Rasoolullah (SAW) forgave all his enemies and declared a general amnesty; he honoured Abu Sufyan, his worst enemy, by declaring his house a place of safety for whoever took refuge in it.
  • Hazrat Ans Bin Maalik (RA): 'I served the Rasoolullah (SAW) for 10 years. By Allah, he never objected to anything I said or did.'
  • The stormy night: The six people spent the whole night standing in the little hut, because there was only one small bed and hardly any room; they chatted and praised the kindness of their host, the old man.
  • Causes of road accidents: over speeding and rash driving; mobile phones while driving; not wearing seat belts; not wearing safety helmets; violating traffic signals, lane discipline and traffic signs. Almost 80% of accidents take place due to the mistake or negligence of drivers.

Abdul Sattar Edhi — The Passage

  • Abdul Sattar Edhi is one of the great personalities of Pakistan, known for his work for the welfare of human beings. He was a great humanitarian, the founder and chairperson of the Edhi Foundation, rightly called 'The Richest Poor Man' and 'Angel of Mercy'.
  • He was born in 1928 in Gujrat, India, and died in 2016 in Karachi, Pakistan.
  • The Edhi Foundation is running the world's largest volunteer ambulance service.
  • Contributions: he laid the foundation of Edhi centers throughout Pakistan; established orphanage homes and rehabilitation centers; his foundation runs the world's largest volunteer ambulance service. He started his charitable work in 1957 during the Asian Flu pandemic and worked for more than 55 years for humanity, leading a simple life far from luxuries; his wife Bilqees Edhi stood by him, and after his death his son Faisal Edhi took charge.

Contextual Meanings

  • welfare — the health, happiness and good of people. charity — help, especially money, given freely to the poor and needy.
  • pandemic — a disease that spreads all over the world. orphan — a child whose parents are dead.
  • mercy — kindness and forgiveness shown towards people who are suffering. humanitarian — a person who works for the welfare of human beings.
  • donation — money or goods given to help a person or organisation. luxurious — very comfortable and expensive; full of luxuries.

options: A great humanitarian and the founder of the Edhi Foundation
mcqs.why: The passage calls Edhi a great humanitarian, founder and chairperson of the Edhi Foundation, known for the welfare of human beings.

mcqs.q: Abdul Sattar Edhi is rightly called ______.
options: 'The Richest Poor Man' and 'Angel of Mercy'
mcqs.why: The passage gives him both titles: 'The Richest Poor Man' and 'Angel of Mercy'.

mcqs.q: Where was Edhi born?
mcqs.why: The passage states he was born in 1928 in Gujrat, India, and died in 2016 in Karachi, Pakistan.

mcqs.q: Which organisation runs the world's largest volunteer ambulance service?
mcqs.why: The Edhi Foundation (Edhi organisation) runs the world's largest volunteer ambulance service under its name.

mcqs.q: When did Edhi start his charitable work?
options: In 1957, during the Asian Flu pandemic
mcqs.why: He started his charitable work in 1957 during the Asian Flu pandemic and worked for more than 55 years for humanity.

mcqs.q: After Edhi's death, who took charge of his work?
mcqs.why: His wife Bilqees Edhi stood by him in his life; after his death, his son Faisal Edhi took charge of the work.

mcqs.q: 'Pandemic' means ______.
options: a disease that spreads all over the world
mcqs.why: The contextual meanings define a pandemic as a disease that spreads all over the world, like the Asian Flu of 1957.

mcqs.q: 'Humanitarian' means ______.
options: a person who collects donations only
a person who works for the welfare of human beings
mcqs.why: A humanitarian is a person who works for the welfare of human beings — the word used for Edhi in the passage.

mcqs.q: How did the six people spend the stormy night in the hut?
options: Sleeping on the one bed by turns
Standing in the little hut, chatting and praising their host's kindness
mcqs.why: There was only one small bed and hardly any room, so all six stood all night, chatting and praising the old man's kindness.

mcqs.q: Edhi's life was ______.
mcqs.why: The passage says he led a simple life far from luxuries; 'luxurious' means very comfortable and expensive, full of luxuries.

lessons.title: Vocabulary and Grammar Review
lessons.notes_html:
Diphthongs in 'The Very Loud Mouse'

The diphthong /au/ (as in 'loud') appears in: loud, mouse, house, cow, down, proud, around, Wow. The diphthong /ia/ (as in 'ear') appears in: hear.

Plural Endings

  • With 's': slides, stars, houses, rivers.
  • With 'es': wishes, crashes, classes, foxes, lunches.
  • With 'ies' (y changed into ies): spies, babies, ladies, parties, memories, stories, countries.

Countable and Uncountable Nouns

  • Countable: mangoes, carrots, tables, houses, fish, flower, cake, apple, dress, lemon, grapes, cup.
  • Uncountable: sand, salt, air, fruit, bread, butter, snow, juice, sugar, rice, cheese, money, grass, oil, meat.

Pronouns in the Dialogue (Waniya and Mahrukh)

'Here is your notebook.' 'Why is it torn?' 'My younger brother did this.' 'It is your responsibility to keep it safe.' 'I have taped the torn pages.' 'Next time, I will not give you anything of mine.' 'I asked you to keep my notebook safe. You did not keep your promise.' 'We should keep our promises. If not, we will lose our trust.'

Verb Forms

Usman is talking on the phone. Somebody opened up the window an hour ago. The birds are flying around the flowers. I am waiting for the bus. Minal and Sameer visit their grandparents in vacations. He is writing a letter. You told me about the painting. Last night, we listened to some noises. Wahaj and Sami are sitting under the tree. Grandmother cooked the dinner last Sunday. (Present continuous for actions happening now; simple past for finished actions marked by 'an hour ago', 'last night', 'last Sunday'.)

Articles

I am a college student. Kiran is the best student in the class. The camel is the ship of the desert. This book has won a prize. I met a boy in the store. Gold is a precious metal. She returned after an hour. There is an institution for the blind in this city. The sun rises in the east. He is the oldest member of the club. (Superlatives 'best' and 'oldest' take 'the'.)

Syllables and Compound Nouns

triangle: tri-an-gle. dictionary: dic-tion-ar-y. watermelon: wa-ter-mel-on. avocado: av-o-ca-do. independent: in-de-pen-dent. February: Feb-ru-ar-y. important: im-por-tant. grandmother: grand-moth-er. misunderstand: mis-un-der-stand. institution: in-sti-tu-tion. December: De-cem-ber. Five compound nouns from the list: watermelon (water + melon), grandmother (grand + mother), butterfly (butter + fly), afternoon (after + noon), underwater (under + water); also anybody (any + body).

mcqs.q: Which diphthong is heard again and again in 'The Very Loud Mouse'?
mcqs.why: Almost every line carries the /au/ sound: loud, mouse, house, cow, down, proud, around, Wow; only 'hear' carries /ia/.

mcqs.q: What is the plural of 'spy'?
mcqs.why: Nouns ending in consonant + y change y into ies: spy–spies, baby–babies, lady–ladies, party–parties, story–stories, country–countries.

mcqs.q: Which noun is uncountable?
mcqs.why: The sorting exercise places rice with sand, salt, air, bread, butter, snow, juice, sugar, cheese, money, grass, oil and meat as uncountable.

mcqs.q: Somebody ______ up the window an hour ago.
mcqs.why: 'An hour ago' marks a finished past action, so the simple past 'opened' is used.

mcqs.q: Usman ______ on the phone.
mcqs.why: The action is happening now, so the present continuous 'is talking' is correct, like 'The birds are flying' and 'I am waiting for the bus.'

mcqs.q: Kiran is ______ best student in the class.

lessons.title: Writing: Paragraph and Mind Map — 'Be Helpful'
lessons.notes_html:
Model Paragraph — A Small Effort That Made Me Feel Special

(Adjectives used: old, poor, heavy, happy, proud.) 'Last Sunday I saw an old, poor woman standing at the busy crossing with a heavy bag. She looked weak and worried. I helped her cross the road and carried her bag to her small house. She gave me a warm smile and prayed for me with kind words. Her sweet prayers made me feel very happy and proud. That small effort taught me that helping others is the greatest joy in life.'

Mind Map — 'Be Helpful'

  • Central topic: Be Helpful.
  • Characters: a kind schoolboy, an old blind man, a shopkeeper.
  • Setting: a busy road near the school, in the morning.
  • Problem: The old blind man wants to cross the busy road but fast traffic does not stop; he is afraid and helpless.
  • Solution: The schoolboy holds his hand, stops the traffic by raising his hand, and takes him safely across; he also carries his basket to his home.
  • Theme: Helping others in trouble is a great virtue; a small act of kindness makes life beautiful and earns love and prayers.

lessons.title: Reading: Hazrat Umar (RA)
lessons.notes_html:
The Title 'Faruq'

The title of Hazrat Umar (RA) is 'Faruq' — the one who distinguishes between right and wrong. He received the title of 'Faruq' after he embraced Islam.

His Reforms

He introduced a great system of administration which served as a model for the Islamic world. His reforms included administrative courts to investigate the complaints against the offices of the state, and he reformed the army, the police force and the tax system. The worship places and property of the non-Muslims were also given protection during his reign. He remained Caliph for ten and a half years and conquered a vast empire during his Khilafat.

His Justice

He gave great importance to justice and the well-being of the people. He would not spare anyone in the case of judgement; for him, high and low, rich and poor were all equal before law. He followed the saying of the Rasoolullah (SAW): 'Treat your servant as you would treat yourself. The master and the servant are both equal before Allah Almighty.'

The Widow's House

One night, passing by a house, he heard children crying. A pot of water was on the fire, and the mother — a widow whose husband had died — was telling the children to go to sleep and that she would wake them when the food was ready; but there was nothing to eat, and no money and grain in the house. Hazrat Umar (RA) helped the widow with food, money and clothing.

Theme of the Text

The main theme: Hazrat Umar (RA) is the model of a just and caring ruler. Paragraph themes: Para 1 — his birth at Makkah in the noble tribe of Quraish, the title 'Faruq', his abilities, and the value of his conversion. Para 2 — his Khilafat, conquests and reforms. Para 3 — his justice: all equal before law. Para 4 — his kindness to the poor: the widow's house. Para 5 — his martyrdom: killed by a non-Muslim named Feroze while offering namaz in the masjid; buried near Hazrat Muhammad (SAW) and Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA) in Madina Munawwarah.

Word Meanings

  • embrace — to accept or believe an idea willingly. treat — to deal with someone in a particular way.
  • condition — a state at a particular time. matter — an affair or situation that is thought about.
  • judgement — the act of assessing; a decision of a court. commit — to perform an act (usually wrong).
  • reign — the ruling period of a caliph/king/ruler. swordsman — a man skilled in the use of swords.

mcqs.q: What is the title of Hazrat Umar (RA)?
options: 'Faruq' — the one who distinguishes between right and wrong
mcqs.why: His title is 'Faruq', the one who distinguishes between right and wrong, received after he embraced Islam.

mcqs.q: How long did Hazrat Umar (RA) remain Caliph?
mcqs.why: The text and the dictation paragraph both state that he remained Caliph for ten and a half years and conquered a vast empire.

options: Administrative courts to investigate complaints against the offices of the state
mcqs.why: His reforms included administrative courts for complaints against state offices, and reforms of the army, police force and tax system.

mcqs.q: During his reign, the worship places and property of non-Muslims were ______.
mcqs.why: The text states that the worship places and property of the non-Muslims were also given protection during his reign.

mcqs.q: How did Hazrat Umar (RA) administer justice?
options: High and low, rich and poor were all equal before law; he spared no one in judgement
He judged only the poor strictly
mcqs.why: He would not spare anyone in the case of judgement; for him, high and low, rich and poor were all equal before law.

mcqs.q: What did the Caliph hear while passing by the poor widow's house?
mcqs.why: He heard children crying; the widow had only a pot of water on the fire and nothing to eat in the house.

mcqs.q: How did Hazrat Umar (RA) help the widow?
options: With a job in the court
mcqs.why: He helped the widow with food, money and clothing — the example of his kindness and sympathy for the poor.

mcqs.q: Who killed Hazrat Umar (RA)?
options: A non-Muslim named Feroze, while he was offering namaz
No one; he died of illness
mcqs.why: Paragraph 5 records his martyrdom: killed by a non-Muslim named Feroze while offering namaz in the masjid.

mcqs.q: Where is Hazrat Umar (RA) buried?
options: In Madina Munawwarah, near Hazrat Muhammad (SAW) and Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA)
mcqs.why: He lies buried in Madina Munawwarah near Hazrat Muhammad (SAW) and Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA).

options: a state at a particular time
