lessons.title: Vocabulary: Silent Letters, Idioms and Proverbs
lessons.notes_html:
Silent Letter Hunt

Words with silent letters in the story: knitting — silent K; wrap/wrapping — silent W; knee — silent K; wrist — silent W; knew — silent K; knob (door knob) — silent K; wrench — silent W. (The mother is knitting; the gift is being wrapped; the butterfly lands on the narrator's knee and wrist.)

Idioms

An idiom is a group of words in a fixed order that has a particular meaning different from the meaning of each word on its own.

  • Better late than never — it is better to do something late than never do it at all.
  • Let's call it a day — let us stop working for today.
  • Under the weather — feeling ill or unwell.
  • The ball is in your court — it is now your turn to take action or make a decision.
  • Spill the beans — to reveal a secret carelessly.
  • Break a leg — good luck! (said especially to a performer).
  • Pull someone's leg — to tease or joke with someone.
  • Sat on the fence — avoided taking sides in a dispute.
  • Through thick and thin — through good times and bad times; in all circumstances.
  • Once in a blue moon — very rarely; almost never.
  • Book examples: give someone a cold shoulder — to ignore someone; a piece of cake — something very easy to do.

Proverbs

A proverb is a short well-known sentence or saying that states a general truth about life.

  • A bird in hand is worth two in the bush.
  • Look before you leap.
  • Birds of a feather flock together.
  • A stitch in time saves nine.
  • All that glitters is not gold.
  • Blood is thicker than water.
  • Every dog has his day.
  • Every dark cloud has a silver lining.
  • Charity begins at home.
  • People who live in glass houses shouldn't throw stones at others.

mcqs.why: The idioms exercise defines 'spill the beans' as revealing a secret carelessly.

mcqs.why: This idiom means the next action or decision is yours — it comes from the idea of the ball being on your side of the court.

mcqs.why: The idiom 'once in a blue moon' means very rarely; almost never.

mcqs.why: The proverb is 'A stitch in time saves nine' — a small repair made in time prevents bigger damage.

mcqs.q: Complete the proverb: 'Birds of a ______ flock together.'
mcqs.why: The proverb is 'Birds of a feather flock together' — people of similar nature keep company with each other.

mcqs.why: The proverb exercise completes it as 'Charity begins at home.'

options: a short well-known saying that states a general truth about life

a word with a silent letter
a sentence that asks a question

lessons.title: Grammar: Kinds of Sentences, Homographs, Homophones and Present Perfect
lessons.notes_html:
Kinds of Sentences

  • Declarative — gives a statement: 'My class teacher will retire in the next month.'
  • Interrogative — asks a question: 'Who is knocking at the door?'
  • Imperative — makes a request or gives an order: 'Let me finish my work.' 'Please give me your camera for two days.'
  • Exclamatory — expresses strong emotion: 'Hurrah! we have won the match.' 'How beautiful this flower is!'

Homographs

Homographs are words with the same spellings and pronunciation but different meanings (book examples: rock, present, watch, right, bear).

  • bat — (a) A bat flew out of the cave at night. (b) He hit the ball with a cricket bat.
  • bank — (a) We sat on the bank of the river. (b) He keeps his money in a bank.
  • light — (a) Please turn off the light. (b) This bag is very light.
  • match — (a) Pakistan won the cricket match. (b) He lit the stove with a match.
  • park — (a) Children are playing in the park. (b) Do not park your car here.

Homophones

Homophones are words with different spellings and meanings but the same sound (e.g. ate/eight, air/heir, buy/bye, brake/break).

  • pale (light-coloured face) — pail (a bucket).
  • see (to look) — sea (ocean).
  • read (past of read) — red (the colour).
  • would (helping verb) — wood (timber).
  • threw (past of throw) — through (from one side to the other).
  • hare (a wild animal like a rabbit) — hair (that grows on the head).

Present Perfect and Present Perfect Continuous

Present perfect: has/have + third form of the verb, for an act completed by now or continuing up to now. Present perfect continuous: has/have been + -ing form, for an action begun in the past and still continuing. 'For' is used with a period of time (for five months); 'since' with the start of a period (since March, since 2019).

  • She has been looking for her watch for two hours, but she has not found it yet.
  • I have been waiting for you since 3 o'clock.
  • The maid has finished her work. He has already left for England.
  • He has been working as the editor of this newspaper since 1990.

mcqs.q: 'Who is knocking at the door?' is a/an ______ sentence.
mcqs.why: An interrogative sentence asks a question; a declarative sentence gives a statement, and an exclamatory sentence expresses strong emotion.

mcqs.q: 'Hurrah! we have won the match.' is a/an ______ sentence.
mcqs.why: It expresses a strong emotion of joy, so it is an exclamatory sentence — like 'How beautiful this flower is!'

mcqs.q: Homographs are words with ______.
options: the same sound but different spellings
the same spellings and pronunciation but different meanings
mcqs.why: Homographs share spelling and pronunciation but differ in meaning: bat (animal) and bat (cricket); bank (river) and bank (money).

mcqs.q: Homophones are words with ______.
options: the same spelling but different meanings
different spellings and meanings but the same sound
mcqs.why: Homophones sound the same but are spelled differently and mean differently: pale/pail, see/sea, threw/through.

mcqs.q: Which pair are homophones?
mcqs.why: Pale (light-coloured face) and pail (a bucket) sound the same with different spellings — homophones. Bat/bat and bank/bank are homographs.

mcqs.q: She ______ for her watch for two hours, but she ______ it yet.
options: has been looking — has not found
mcqs.why: A continuing action takes the present perfect continuous (has been looking); a result not achieved by now takes the present perfect (has not found).

mcqs.q: I ______ for you since 3 o'clock in the afternoon.
mcqs.why: 'Since 3 o'clock' marks an action begun in the past and still continuing — the present perfect continuous 'have been waiting'.

mcqs.q: 'For' is used with ______ and 'since' with ______.
options: the start of a period — a period of time
a period of time — the start of a period
mcqs.why: The book's rule: 'for' with a period of time (for five months); 'since' with the start of a period (since March, since 2019).

mcqs.q: He ______ as the editor of this newspaper since 1990.
mcqs.why: Working since 1990 and still continuing requires the present perfect continuous: has been working.

mcqs.q: 'Please give me your camera for two days' is a/an ______ sentence.
mcqs.why: Imperative sentences make requests or give orders; 'Please give me...' is a polite request, like 'Let me finish my work.'

lessons.title: Writing: Summary, Reforms and Essay on Justice
lessons.notes_html:
Summary of the Text 'Hazrat Umar (RA)'

(Steps: read carefully, identify main divisions, jot down keywords, be objective, sum up in your own words.) Hazrat Umar (RA) was the second Caliph of Islam. Born at Makkah Mukarramah in the noble tribe of Quraish, he was a tall, strong and brave man, a good wrestler, horse-rider and swordsman, and one of the few persons in Makkah who could read and write. After embracing Islam he received the title 'Faruq', and his conversion greatly strengthened the Rasoolullah (SAW) in his mission. He remained Caliph for ten and a half years, conquered a vast empire and introduced a model system of administration, with reforms in the courts, army, police force and tax system, and protection for non-Muslims. He was famous for justice — high and low, rich and poor were equal before law — and for his care of the poor, whom he visited in disguise at night, as in the case of the hungry widow and her children, whom he helped with food, money and clothing. He was martyred by a non-Muslim, Feroze, while offering namaz, and lies buried in Madina Munawwarah near Hazrat Muhammad (SAW) and Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA).

Model — Reforms I Would Bring as a Ruler

'If I became the ruler of my country, I would first make justice quick and equal for rich and poor, like Hazrat Umar (RA). I would set up complaint courts against corrupt officers. I would make education free for every child and build hospitals in every town. I would reform the police so that they protect the people, and the tax system so that the rich pay fairly and the poor are helped from the treasury. I would visit the people myself to see their real condition, and I would protect the rights of minorities. My aim would be a country where no one sleeps hungry.'

Essay — 'Importance of Justice' (Model)

Mind map: Centre — Importance of Justice. Branches: (1) Equality — all are equal before law. (2) Peace — no revenge and no fighting. (3) Trust — people trust rulers and courts. (4) Progress — trade and work flourish. (5) Example — Hazrat Umar (RA). Justice is the foundation of a peaceful society. Where justice is done, no one takes the law into his own hands, so crime and revenge disappear. People trust their rulers and courts, work honestly and the country progresses. On the other hand, injustice creates hatred, unrest and weakness in a nation.

mcqs.why: The summary begins: 'Hazrat Umar (RA) was the second Caliph of Islam', after Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA).

mcqs.q: According to the summary, Hazrat Umar (RA) was one of the few persons in Makkah who could ______.
mcqs.why: He was a tall, strong and brave man, a good wrestler, horse-rider and swordsman, and one of the few persons in Makkah who could read and write.

mcqs.q: His conversion to Islam ______.
options: greatly strengthened the Rasoolullah (SAW) in his mission
mcqs.why: The summary states that after embracing Islam he received the title 'Faruq', and his conversion greatly strengthened the Rasoolullah (SAW) in his mission.

mcqs.q: In the summary, he visited the poor ______.
mcqs.why: He cared for the poor, whom he visited in disguise at night — as in the case of the hungry widow and her children.

options: copy the text word for word
mcqs.why: The book's steps for summary writing: read carefully, identify main divisions, jot down keywords, be objective, and sum up in your own words.

mcqs.q: A summary should be written ______.
mcqs.why: The steps require the summary to be objective and summed up in your own words — not copied and not mixed with opinion.

options: justice quick and equal for rich and poor
mcqs.why: 'I would first make justice quick and equal for rich and poor, like Hazrat Umar (RA)' — then complaint courts, free education, hospitals, police and tax reforms.

mcqs.q: In the model reforms, the poor would be helped ______.
mcqs.why: The tax system would be reformed 'so that the rich pay fairly and the poor are helped from the treasury.'

options: no one takes the law into his own hands, so crime and revenge disappear
mcqs.why: The essay says justice brings equality, peace and trust: no one takes the law into his own hands, so crime and revenge disappear.

lessons.title: Reading: Sports and Sportsmanship
lessons.notes_html:
Key Values Learned from Sports

Through participation in sports, young people learn the importance of key values such as honesty, teamwork, fair play, respect for themselves and others, and adherence to rules.

'Sports is Competitive'

It means that in sports the players or teams compete against each other to win. Sports has many breathtaking moments which are a source of joy — some eyes shed tears and some faces smile — but in the end what matters is shaking hands and showcasing sportsmanship.

Character Building

Sports makes a person strong-willed and disciplined. It teaches us to work in a team, which is helpful for collaboration in every walk of life; it builds honesty, integrity, ethical behaviour and goodwill toward opponents. Recent studies show that students who give equal importance to sports along with studies are achievers in professional life. Sports also helps us deal with immense mental pressure and the problems of daily life.

Brian G. on Sportsmanship

'Sportsmanship is an understanding of and commitment to fair play, ethical behaviour and integrity, and general goodwill toward an opponent.' In other words: true sportsmanship means playing fairly and honestly, behaving well, and showing kindness and goodwill even towards the rival team — winning or losing is secondary.

Promoting Sports in Pakistan

The Pakistan Sports Board (PSB), under the Ministry of Inter Provincial Coordination, is the premier authority for promoting sports in the country. At present forty-one National Sports Federations and three departments are affiliated with the Board. Each Federation is responsible for the promotion and development of its respective sport. The Board has sporting facilities at its Coaching Centers at Provincial Headquarters, used for national training camps and national and international competitions.

Word Meanings

  • fundamental — something of central importance. adherence — attachment or commitment (to rules).
  • showcasing — exhibiting; displaying. collaboration — cooperation.
  • immense — very great. extraordinary — very unusual or remarkable.
  • inauguration — the beginning or introduction of a system. prestigious — inspiring respect and admiration; having high status.
  • significant — important; worthy of attention. consecutive — following each other continuously.
  • affiliated — officially attached or connected to an organisation.

mcqs.why: The text lists the key values: honesty, teamwork, fair play, respect for themselves and others, and adherence to rules.

lessons.title: Reading Skills: Fact and Opinion, Super Star Fact File
lessons.notes_html:
Fact and Opinion

A fact is a true statement that you can prove; an opinion is someone's idea or feeling about something.

  • Facts in the text: Hockey is the national game of Pakistan; Pakistan won the Cricket World Cup 1992, ICC World Twenty20 in 2009 and ICC Champions Trophy 2017; Pakistan won the Asian Games hockey title six times; Jahangir Khan remained unbeaten after 555 consecutive matches; Kiran Baloch holds the world record of the highest score (242 runs) in a women's Test match; forty-one National Sports Federations are affiliated with the PSB.
  • Opinions of the author: 'Cricket is not only a sport for Pakistanis but also an emotion'; 'Pakistani women are, without a doubt, the most talented ladies in the world'; sports and physical education are fundamental to healthy development.

Super Star Fact File — Jahangir Khan (Model)

  • Name: Jahangir Khan. Sport: Squash.
  • Age: Born on 10 December 1963 in Karachi.
  • Height: about 5 feet 10 inches. Weight: about 68 kg.
  • Playing style: Extremely fast, powerful and tireless; famous for his fitness and long rallies.
  • Interesting fact: He remained unbeaten even after 555 consecutive matches — the greatest winning streak in sports history — and Pakistan has the record of winning 17 World Opens in squash.
  • Why I admire him: He brought unmatched honour to Pakistan through hard work, discipline and sportsmanship, and remained humble at the top.

options: He brought unmatched honour to Pakistan through hard work, discipline and sportsmanship, and remained humble
mcqs.why: The model answer: he brought unmatched honour to Pakistan through hard work, discipline and sportsmanship, and remained humble at the top.

mcqs.q: A fact file of a sportsman includes ______.
options: name, sport, age, height, weight, playing style and interesting facts
mcqs.why: The activity's points are: Name, Sport, Age, Weight, Height, Playing style, Interesting fact, and why you admire the sportsman.

lessons.title: Vocabulary: Cloze Paragraph, Abbreviations and Acronyms
lessons.notes_html:
Cloze Paragraph — Basketball

'Did you know that basketball was first played in 1891? A man from Canada invented it. He was a college teacher. His name was James Naismith. Mr Naismith had a reason for making up this game. He had to think of a game to play indoors in winter. His idea for basketball game came from a children's game. It was called 'Duck on a Flock'. Mr Naismith changed it a little. He got peach baskets. They were used to hold peaches. He nailed the empty baskets to the walls of the gym. Later on, Mr Naismith cut the bottoms out of the baskets. The way the balls would pass through.'

Abbreviations and Acronyms

Abbreviations are shortened or contracted forms of words and expressions we use every day (book examples: St. = street; Mon., Tues., Wed.; Jan., Feb., Aug.; cm = centimeters; vs = versus). An acronym is a word formed from the initial letters of a longer name or phrase and pronounced as a word (book examples: RADAR, SCUBA, NASA, LASER, SIM card, ZIP code).

  • Five more: Dr. — Doctor (abbreviation); Mr. — Mister (abbreviation); kg — kilogram (abbreviation); etc. — et cetera, 'and so on' (abbreviation); UNESCO — United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (acronym); PIN — Personal Identification Number (acronym).

mcqs.q: Basketball was first played in ______.
mcqs.why: The cloze paragraph begins: 'Did you know that basketball was first played in 1891?'

mcqs.q: Who invented basketball?
options: James Naismith, a college teacher from Canada
mcqs.why: A man from Canada invented it; he was a college teacher named James Naismith.

mcqs.q: Why did Naismith invent basketball?
options: He wanted a game for the beach
He was ordered by a king
He needed a game to play indoors in winter
mcqs.why: He had to think of a game to play indoors in winter; his idea came from a children's game called 'Duck on a Flock'.

mcqs.q: What did Naismith use as the first baskets?
options: Peach baskets nailed to the walls of the gym
mcqs.why: He got peach baskets — used to hold peaches — and nailed the empty baskets to the walls of the gym.

mcqs.q: Why did Naismith cut the bottoms out of the baskets?
options: So that the balls would pass through
mcqs.why: Later he cut the bottoms out of the baskets so that the balls would pass through — the cloze words are used exactly once each.

mcqs.q: An acronym is ______.
options: a shortened form of a single word
a word formed from the initial letters of a longer name or phrase, pronounced as a word
a word with a silent letter
mcqs.why: NASA, LASER and UNESCO are acronyms — formed from initial letters and pronounced as words; Dr., kg and etc. are abbreviations.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an acronym?
mcqs.why: UNESCO stands for United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization and is pronounced as a word — an acronym. Dr., kg and etc. are abbreviations.

mcqs.q: 'etc.' is an abbreviation of ______.
mcqs.why: The exercise gives etc. — et cetera, meaning 'and so on', as an abbreviation used every day.

mcqs.q: PIN stands for ______.
mcqs.why: PIN — Personal Identification Number — is listed as an acronym; SIM card and ZIP code are the book's other examples.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an abbreviation?
mcqs.why: The book's examples of abbreviations include cm = centimeters, St. = street and vs = versus; NASA, LASER and RADAR are acronyms.

lessons.title: Grammar: Adverbs, Adverb Phrases and Clauses, Past Perfect
lessons.notes_html:
Adverbs

An adverb modifies a verb, an adjective or another adverb. Adverbs of manner tell the way people do things; adverbs of time tell when; adverbs of place tell where the action takes place. Adjectives to adverbs: strong — strongly; brave — bravely; soft — softly; quiet — quietly; slow — slowly.

  • 'Ahmad, you can stay outside.' — outside: adverb of place.
  • 'The sun is shining brightly.' — brightly: adverb of manner.
  • 'Sana arrived late.' — late: adverb of time.
  • 'It rained heavily last night.' — heavily: manner; last night: time.
  • 'The principal seriously considered my suggestion.' — seriously: manner.

Adverb Phrases

An adverb phrase, like an adverb, modifies verbs or other adverbs. A phrase is a group of words that does not give a complete sense, while a clause has its own subject and predicate. Solved: There were no windows inside the room. They started to cross the street without looking. From the balcony he could see the sea. He ran by the lake. Frogs make all sorts of noises near the creek.

Adverb Clauses

An adverb clause is a group of words which contains a subject and predicate of its own and does the work of an adverb; adverb clauses answer how, when, where or why about the verb (e.g. 'When students play regularly, their health improves'; 'We exercise daily so that we may stay fit'; 'I love hockey because it teaches teamwork').

Past Perfect and Past Perfect Continuous

Past perfect: an action completed before a certain moment in the past — if two actions happened in the past, the earlier one takes the past perfect. Past perfect continuous: an action that began before a certain point in the past and continued up to that time — had been + -ing form.

  • The rain had stopped before I reached home.
  • The building had burnt down before the fire brigade arrived.
  • It had been raining since midnight.
  • The mechanics had been repairing the engine for the last three hours.
  • Afshan had been waiting for Saima for two hours.

mcqs.q: In 'The sun is shining brightly', 'brightly' is an adverb of ______.
mcqs.why: Brightly tells HOW the sun is shining — an adverb of manner, like slowly, heavily and seriously in the exercise.

mcqs.q: In 'Sana arrived late', 'late' is an adverb of ______.
mcqs.why: Late tells WHEN Sana arrived — an adverb of time; 'last night' is also an adverb of time.

mcqs.q: 'Outside' in 'you can stay outside' is an adverb of ______.
mcqs.why: Outside tells WHERE the action takes place — an adverb of place, like here and there.

mcqs.q: What is the adverb form of 'brave'?
options: brave-ly with one e dropped wrongly as 'bravly'
mcqs.why: Adjectives change to adverbs with -ly: strong–strongly, brave–bravely, soft–softly, quiet–quietly, slow–slowly.

mcqs.q: An adverb phrase ______.
options: always has its own subject and predicate
modifies verbs or other adverbs, like an adverb
mcqs.why: An adverb phrase does the work of an adverb; unlike a clause, a phrase does not give a complete sense and has no subject–predicate pair of its own.

mcqs.q: 'Frogs make all sorts of noises ______.'
mcqs.why: The solved adverb-phrase exercise completes the sentence with 'near the creek'; the balcony phrase completes 'he could see the sea'.

mcqs.q: An adverb clause differs from an adverb phrase because it ______.
options: contains a subject and predicate of its own
mcqs.why: An adverb clause is a group of words with its own subject and predicate doing the work of an adverb, answering how, when, where or why.

mcqs.q: The rain ______ before I reached home.
mcqs.why: Of the two past actions, the earlier one (the rain stopping) takes the past perfect: had stopped.

mcqs.q: It ______ since midnight. (past perfect continuous)
mcqs.why: An action that began before a past point and continued up to it takes had been + -ing: had been raining.

mcqs.q: The building ______ down before the fire brigade arrived.
mcqs.why: The burning was completed before the brigade arrived, so the past perfect 'had burnt' is used for the earlier action.

lessons.title: Writing: Essay 'My Favourite Sport' and Dialogue
lessons.notes_html:
Essay — 'My Favourite Sport' (Model)

Mind map: Favourite sport — Cricket. Why — it is the most significant sport for Pakistanis; it is not only a sport but an emotion. Where — in the school ground and the street near my house. With whom — class fellows and friends. When — every evening and on Sundays. How — two teams of eleven; one team bats and the other bowls and fields; the team scoring more runs wins. What I learn — teamwork, discipline, fair play and sportsmanship.

Essay: 'My favourite sport is cricket. It is the most popular game in Pakistan and is played in grounds, streets, house yards and roof tops — at any place where a bat can swing and a ball can bounce. I play cricket with my friends every evening in the school ground. Two teams of eleven players take part; one side bats while the other bowls and fields, and the side that scores more runs wins the match. Pakistan has a glorious cricket history — it won the Cricket World Cup in 1992, the ICC World Twenty20 in 2009 and the ICC Champions Trophy in 2017. Cricket teaches me teamwork, patience, discipline and true sportsmanship: to play fair, respect the opponents and accept victory and defeat gracefully.'

Dialogue on a Cricket Match (Model)

Ahmad: Did you watch yesterday's cricket match? Ali: Yes, I watched it with my family. What a breathtaking match it was! Ahmad: Pakistan batted first and scored 180 runs. I thought it was an easy target. Ali: But the last five overs were full of suspense. Our bowlers bowled very well. Ahmad: The final over was the best. We needed one wicket, and our bowler took it on the last ball. Ali: That is sports! Both teams played fair, and in the end they shook hands like true sportsmen. Ahmad: I wish I could play like them one day. Ali: With practice and discipline, you surely can.

mcqs.q: In the model essay, the writer's favourite sport is ______.
mcqs.why: The mind map and essay both name cricket — 'the most significant sport for Pakistanis' and 'not only a sport but an emotion.'

mcqs.q: How many players are there in each cricket team in the essay?
mcqs.why: Two teams of eleven players take part; one side bats while the other bowls and fields.

mcqs.q: How is the winner decided in the essay's description?
options: The side that scores more runs wins the match
The side that takes more wickets always wins
The side that fields first wins
mcqs.why: The essay explains: one team bats, the other bowls and fields, and the side scoring more runs wins.

mcqs.q: What does cricket teach the writer?
options: How to win at any cost
Teamwork, patience, discipline and true sportsmanship
mcqs.why: Cricket teaches him teamwork, patience, discipline and sportsmanship: to play fair, respect opponents and accept victory and defeat gracefully.

mcqs.q: In the model dialogue, Pakistan scored ______ runs.
mcqs.why: Ahmad says: 'Pakistan batted first and scored 180 runs. I thought it was an easy target.'

mcqs.q: In the dialogue, the match was decided ______.
options: on the last ball of the final over, when the bowler took the needed wicket
mcqs.why: Ahmad says the final over was the best: 'We needed one wicket, and our bowler took it on the last ball.'

mcqs.q: Ali says the last five overs were full of ______.
mcqs.why: Ali: 'But the last five overs were full of suspense. Our bowlers bowled very well.'

mcqs.q: At the end of the match in the dialogue, both teams ______.
mcqs.why: Ali says both teams played fair and in the end shook hands like true sportsmen — the sportsmanship theme of the unit.

mcqs.q: The essay's mind map asks: What? Why? Where? Who with? When? How? and ______.
options: What can you learn from it?
mcqs.why: The mind-map points end with 'What can you learn from it?' — answered by teamwork, discipline, fair play and sportsmanship.

mcqs.q: Where does the writer play cricket?
options: In the school ground (and the street near his house)
mcqs.why: The mind map says: in the school ground and the street near my house, with class fellows and friends, every evening and on Sundays.

lessons.title: Reading: The Earth Speaks (Poem)
lessons.notes_html:
The Four Seasons

The Earth has gifted us four seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter. In spring the lilacs bloom; flowers open everywhere, the weather becomes pleasant, new leaves appear on trees and the whole earth looks fresh and green. Autumn comes when the maple turns red. Summer is crowned with sunshine — all bright and warm. Winter brings snow and icicle spears — cold and white. Each season comes 'with all their joys, and all their pleasures and all their fears'.

'All Their Pleasures and All Their Fears'

The Earth means that every season brings both happiness and hardship. The seasons give joys and pleasures — flowers, sunshine, fruits and snow — but they also bring fears and difficulties, such as the severe cold of winter or the heat of summer. We must accept and use both sides of every season.

Using Each Season Wisely and Kindly

We can use each season wisely by doing the work suited to it — sowing in time, harvesting in time, saving water and food — and kindly by caring for the earth: planting trees, keeping our surroundings clean, not wasting nature's gifts, and helping people, animals and plants bear the hardships of each season, so that at the year's last hour we have a worthy record to tell.

'To Use My Gifts as Best You Know'

The Earth wants us to use its four gifts — the four seasons — as best as we know: wisely, kindly and well. The gifts are ours, and ours is the task of using them rightly. We may encourage others by our own example: keeping the surroundings clean, planting trees, saving water, and telling people that the earth is a trust for which we will have to give a worthy record at the end of the year.

Main Idea of the Poem

In this poem by Lenore Hetrick, the Earth itself speaks to human beings. It reminds us that it gives us four seasons, each with its own joys, pleasures and fears. These seasons are gifts, and our task is to use each one wisely, kindly and well, so that we can present a worthy record of our deeds at the end of the year. The poem teaches gratitude and responsibility towards nature.

Word Meanings

  • somber — dark, dull and gloomy; serious. crowned — covered as if with a crown; having on top.
  • icicle — a long, thin, pointed piece of ice hanging from a surface. wisely — in a sensible and careful way, using good judgement.
  • worthy — deserving respect or attention; valuable.

mcqs.q: How many seasons has the Earth gifted us?
options: Four — spring, summer, autumn and winter
mcqs.why: The Earth says, 'Four seasons I give you': spring, summer, autumn and winter, each with its joys, pleasures and fears.

mcqs.q: Spring comes when ______.
mcqs.why: Spring comes when the lilacs bloom; autumn comes when the maple turns red; summer is crowned with sunshine; winter brings snow and icicle spears.

mcqs.q: Summer is described as ______.
options: crowned with sunshine — all bright and warm
mcqs.why: The comprehension answer says summer is crowned with sunshine; 'crowned' means covered as if with a crown, having on top.

mcqs.q: What does the Earth mean by 'all their pleasures and all their fears'?
options: Every season brings both happiness and hardship
mcqs.why: Each season gives joys and pleasures — flowers, sunshine, fruits and snow — but also fears and difficulties, like the cold of winter or the heat of summer.

mcqs.q: How can we use each season wisely?
options: By doing the work suited to it — sowing in time, harvesting in time, saving water and food
mcqs.why: Using a season wisely means work suited to it: sowing and harvesting in time, saving water and food; kindly means caring for the earth.

mcqs.q: What does the Earth want from us in 'To use my gifts as best you know'?
options: To use the four seasons wisely, kindly and well
To sell the gifts of nature
mcqs.why: The gifts are ours, and ours is the task of using them rightly, so that at the year's last hour we have a worthy record to tell.

mcqs.q: Who is the poet of 'The Earth Speaks'?
mcqs.why: The main-idea answer names the poem as by Lenore Hetrick, in which the Earth itself speaks to human beings.

mcqs.q: 'Icicle' means ______.
options: a long, thin, pointed piece of ice hanging from a surface
mcqs.why: The dictionary meanings define an icicle as a long, thin, pointed piece of ice hanging from a surface — winter's 'icicle spears'.

mcqs.q: 'Somber' means ______.
mcqs.why: The turning earth spoke in a somber voice — dark, dull and gloomy; serious. Wisely means in a sensible, careful way.

mcqs.q: The poem teaches ______.
mcqs.why: The main idea concludes: the poem teaches gratitude and responsibility towards nature, using each gift wisely, kindly and well.

lessons.title: Poetry and Vocabulary: Personification, Capitonyms, Denotation and Connotation
lessons.notes_html:
Personification

Personification attributes human characteristics to something non-human. The whole poem is built on personification — the Earth, a non-human thing, is given human qualities: it speaks ('The turning earth spoke in a somber voice'), it has a voice ('its deep voice said'), it gives gifts deliberately ('Four seasons I give you') and it assigns a task to human beings ('yours is the task').

Simile and Metaphor

A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor compares without 'like/as'. Similes from the book's pictures: Her heart is as pure as gold. Her lips are as red as a rose. He is as busy as a bee. The old man is as cunning as a fox. She is as wise as an owl. Our captain is as brave as a lion.

Capitonyms

A capitonym is a word whose meaning changes when it is capitalized. The capitalized form is a proper noun (a place, month or people) while the small-letter form is a common word with a completely different meaning; capitonyms have the same spelling but different meanings, and are a form of homographs.

  • Turkey — a country in Western Asia and Eastern Europe; turkey — a large bird kept for its meat.
  • May — the fifth month; may — a modal verb showing possibility or permission.
  • August — the eighth month; august — respected and impressive; grand.
  • March — the third month; march — to walk with regular, firm steps like a soldier.
  • Polish — relating to Poland, its people or language; polish — a substance used to make something shine.
  • China — a country in East Asia; china — fine white clay plates, cups etc. (porcelain).

Denotation and Connotation

Denotation is the literal, dictionary meaning of a word. Connotation is the feelings and ideas associated with the word, according to context.

  • blue — denotative: 'Alia is wearing a blue shirt today' (a colour). Connotative: 'Alia is blue after her father's death' (sad and depressed).
  • wave — denotative: 'The wave crashes against the beach' (waves of the sea). Connotative: 'He grieved in waves of sadness' (feelings coming again and again).
  • pour — denotative: 'Pour a glass of water' (flow of liquid). Connotative: 'She poured herself into the project' (she became deeply involved in it).

mcqs.q: Personification is ______.
options: a word whose meaning changes when capitalized
giving human characteristics to something non-human
the dictionary meaning of a word
mcqs.why: The whole poem is personification: the Earth speaks, has a voice, gives gifts deliberately and assigns a task to human beings.

mcqs.q: Which line from the poem shows personification?
options: 'In winter, icicles hang from the roof'
'We should use the gifts of nature wisely'
'The turning earth spoke in a somber voice'
mcqs.why: The Earth — a non-human thing — is shown speaking, which is personification; the solved answer quotes this line.

mcqs.q: 'Our captain is as brave as a lion' is a ______.
mcqs.why: A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as' — here bravery is compared with a lion using 'as'.

mcqs.q: A capitonym is a word ______.
options: whose meaning changes when it is capitalized
mcqs.why: Turkey (country) and turkey (bird) are capitonyms: same spelling, different meaning when capitalized; they are a form of homographs.

mcqs.q: 'August' with a capital A means ______, while 'august' means ______.
options: the third month — to walk like a soldier
the eighth month — respected and impressive; grand
mcqs.why: August is the eighth month of the year; august (small a) means respected and impressive, grand.

mcqs.q: 'China' and 'china' differ because ______.
options: china is a country; China is a dish
China is a country in East Asia; china is fine porcelain ware
mcqs.why: The capitonyms exercise: China — a country in East Asia; china — fine white clay plates, cups etc. (porcelain).

mcqs.q: Denotation is ______.
options: the literal, dictionary meaning of a word
the feelings associated with a word
the opposite meaning of a word
mcqs.why: Denotation is the literal dictionary meaning; connotation is the feelings and ideas associated with the word according to context.

mcqs.q: In 'Alia is blue after her father's death', 'blue' is used ______.
options: connotatively — it means sad and depressed
mcqs.why: Here 'blue' does not name the colour; its connotation is sad and depressed. In 'a blue shirt', it is denotative.

mcqs.q: In 'She poured herself into the project', 'poured' means ______.
options: she became deeply involved in it
mcqs.why: This is the connotative use of pour; denotatively, 'Pour a glass of water' means the flow of liquid from one container to another.

mcqs.q: 'Polish' with a capital P relates to ______.
options: a substance used to make something shine
a large bird kept for its meat
mcqs.why: Polish (capital) means relating to Poland, its people or language; polish (small) is a substance used to make something shine.

lessons.title: Grammar: Conjunctions, Transitional Devices and Correlative Conjunctions
lessons.notes_html:
Conjunctions

A conjunction joins words, phrases and clauses. Co-ordinating conjunctions join two independent statements of equal rank: and, but, for, or, nor, so. Subordinating conjunctions join a dependent clause to an independent clause: as, whenever, when, although, because, until, while.

  • Neither Alia nor Mariam has come.
  • She speaks both English and Punjabi. (or: English as well as Punjabi.)
  • I like him because he is very sincere.
  • He did not win although he worked hard.
  • She lost the match, but she is cheerful.
  • Although it was raining, we decided to go out.

Transitional Devices

In the Band-Aid paragraph the transitional words are: 'but', 'During the first week', 'After that', 'Then', 'From then on', 'whenever', 'Soon', 'After four years'. Difference: a conjunction grammatically joins words, phrases or clauses inside sentences. Transitional devices (then, after that, furthermore, in other words, soon) indicate the relationship — time, contrast, addition — between two sentences or paragraphs; they connect ideas rather than joining clauses, and often begin a new sentence.

Correlative Conjunctions

Correlative conjunctions work in pairs to join words, phrases or clauses:

  • whether–or: I do not know whether he will come or stay at home.
  • neither–nor: Neither the teacher nor the students were present.
  • not–but: He is not a singer but a poet.
  • both–and: Both hockey and cricket are famous in Pakistan.
  • either–or: You may either take tea or coffee.
  • not only–but also: She is not only intelligent but also hardworking.

mcqs.q: Join: 'Alia hasn't come. Mariam hasn't come.'
options: Neither Alia nor Mariam has come
mcqs.why: The pair neither–nor joins the two negative statements: 'Neither Alia nor Mariam has come.'

mcqs.q: 'He did not win ______ he worked hard.'
mcqs.why: The solved joining uses the subordinating conjunction 'although' for contrast: 'He did not win although he worked hard.'

mcqs.q: 'I like him ______ he is very sincere.'
mcqs.why: A reason is given, so 'because' joins the sentences: 'I like him because he is very sincere.'

mcqs.q: Co-ordinating conjunctions join ______.
options: two independent statements of equal rank
a dependent clause to an independent clause
mcqs.why: And, but, for, or, nor, so are co-ordinating conjunctions joining equals; although, because, when and while are subordinating conjunctions.

mcqs.q: Transitional devices differ from conjunctions because they ______.
options: connect ideas between sentences or paragraphs rather than joining clauses
change the tense of a verb
mcqs.why: Transitional devices like 'then', 'after that' and 'soon' indicate relationships between sentences and often begin a new sentence; conjunctions join clauses grammatically.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a transitional device in the Band-Aid paragraph?
mcqs.why: The paragraph's transitional words include 'During the first week', 'After that', 'Then', 'From then on', 'Soon' and 'After four years'.

mcqs.q: Correlative conjunctions ______.
options: work in pairs to join words, phrases or clauses
mcqs.why: Whether–or, neither–nor, both–and, either–or and not only–but also work in pairs — that is why they are called correlative.

mcqs.q: 'She is ______ intelligent ______ hardworking.'
mcqs.why: The solved sentence is: 'She is not only intelligent but also hardworking.'

mcqs.q: 'You may ______ take tea ______ coffee.'
mcqs.why: Either–or offers a choice between two things: 'You may either take tea or coffee.'

mcqs.q: '______ it was raining, we decided to go out.'
mcqs.why: Contrast requires 'Although': 'Although it was raining, we decided to go out.'

lessons.title: Grammar: Future Tenses and Modal Verbs
lessons.notes_html:
Future Tenses

Simple future: shall/will + first form of the verb — used for things we cannot control and for what we think will happen; the 'going to' form is used for decisions taken just before speaking. Future continuous: will be/shall be + -ing form — an action that will be in progress at some future moment.

  • He will be waiting for us at the station.
  • I shall return from Murree this evening.
  • I shall be finishing the book in an hour's time.
  • He will not understand my point.
  • The project will cost a lot of money.
  • He will be working regularly from the next month.
  • I shall be travelling by air tomorrow.
  • They will grow wheat this year.

Modal Verbs

Modal verbs are auxiliary verbs that express necessity or possibility: must, shall, will, should, would, can, could, may, might.

  • You have enough clothes for summer. You need not buy more.
  • It may rain tomorrow according to the weather forecast.
  • We should do morning walk to keep ourselves healthy.
  • Tahira can win the competition as she worked hard.
  • I can read well, but cannot write a good essay.

mcqs.q: He ______ for us at the station. (future continuous)
mcqs.why: An action that will be in progress at a future moment takes the future continuous: will be + -ing — 'He will be waiting for us at the station.'

mcqs.q: I ______ by air tomorrow. (future continuous)
mcqs.why: Travelling tomorrow will be in progress at a future moment: 'I shall be travelling by air tomorrow.'

mcqs.q: The project ______ a lot of money. (simple future)
mcqs.why: The simple future is shall/will + first form of the verb: 'The project will cost a lot of money.'

mcqs.q: The simple future is used for ______.
options: things we cannot control and what we think will happen
mcqs.why: The book states the simple future (shall/will + first form) is used for things we cannot control and for what we think will happen.

mcqs.q: 'You have enough clothes for summer. You ______ buy more.'
mcqs.why: Having enough clothes, there is no necessity to buy more: 'You need not (needn't) buy more.'

mcqs.q: 'It ______ rain tomorrow according to weather forecast.'
mcqs.why: A forecast shows possibility, so the modal is 'may': 'It may rain tomorrow.'

mcqs.q: 'We ______ do morning walk to keep ourselves healthy.'
mcqs.why: 'Should' expresses advice/duty: we should do morning walk to keep ourselves healthy.

mcqs.q: 'Tahira ______ win the competition as she worked hard.'
mcqs.why: 'Can' expresses ability/possibility earned by hard work: Tahira can win the competition.

mcqs.q: Modal verbs are auxiliary verbs that express ______.
mcqs.why: The book defines modal verbs as auxiliary verbs expressing necessity or possibility: must, shall, will, should, would, can, could, may, might.

mcqs.q: I ______ from Murree this evening. (simple future)
mcqs.why: With 'I', the simple future is 'shall return' — shall + first form of the verb.

lessons.title: Writing: Paragraph, Poem Summary and Own Poem
lessons.notes_html:
Paragraph — 'Myself After Ten Years' (Model)

'After ten years, I will be a doctor serving in a government hospital of my city. I shall have completed my MBBS and will be treating poor patients who cannot afford costly treatment. I will open a small free clinic in my village so that people may get help near their homes. I should work hard from today, because only hard work can turn this dream into reality. I will also teach poor children in the evening, for education can change their future. I believe that if I stay honest and determined, I shall surely succeed, and my parents will be proud of me.'

Summary of the Poem 'The Earth Speaks'

'The Earth Speaks' is a poem by Lenore Hetrick. In it, the turning Earth speaks in a somber, deep voice and addresses human beings. The Earth says that it gives us four seasons: spring when the lilacs bloom, autumn when the maple is red, summer crowned with sunshine, and winter of snow and icicle spears. It gives these four gifts with all their joys, pleasures and fears, and asks us to take them and use each one wisely, kindly and well, so that at the year's last hour we may present a worthy record. The Earth speaks once again in a low voice: the gifts are ours, and ours is the task to use them as best we know.

Own Poem — 'The Little Bandage' (Model, on the invention of Band-Aid)

'Josephine's hands were always red with cuts, / As sharp knives played their tricks each day; / Her husband watched her wounds with a worried heart, / And dreamed of driving her pain away. / He cut the tape like ribbons of hope, / And placed soft gauze, a tiny white bed; / "This little shield will guard her skin," / The kind inventor proudly said. / Soon the small bandage flew to every home, / Like a hero it heals the wounds so small; / The Band-Aid, born of love and care, / Is a friend in need for one and all.' Figurative language used: personification — knives 'played tricks', the bandage is a 'hero' and a 'friend'; metaphor — 'ribbons of hope', 'a tiny white bed', 'this little shield'.

lessons.title: Poem 'Anger' and Reading: Settling the Quarrel
lessons.notes_html:
Poem 'Anger' by Debbie Palphreyman — Oral Answers

  • The narrator is a young child (a schoolboy) describing his own anger and how he controls it.
  • Jason pushed him into the wall; Sophie said he wasn't very tall; Adam called him a very rude name. These acts made him angry.
  • If he acted rash, he could do something foolish: give someone a great big bash, or kick and hurt someone he knows; he might damage something special to himself, such as a boot or a shoe when kicking a tree — and afterwards he would feel very low.
  • He would calm himself by counting to ten (CALM — count to ten), hiding in a den, running very fast so the anger won't last, breathing slow and deep, or even having a weep.
  • It is important to be calm so that we do not hurt others, property or ourselves, and so that others do not fear us.
  • If someone bothers us: do not react rashly; stay calm, count to ten, breathe deeply, and settle the matter peacefully by talking.

The Story — Why Haji Usman Was Respected

Haji Usman was a wise old man who lived in a little village near Faisalabad. The villagers respected him very much for his piety, sought his advice on various matters, and he many times acted as a conciliator to settle quarrels.

The Quarrel

Salman had accidentally destroyed some of Haroon's crops by driving his tractor through Haroon's fields. Haroon wanted Salman to pay for his loss. Salman blamed Haroon: Haroon's unguarded sheep had suddenly run onto the road, and to avoid hitting them Salman had steered into the fields and smashed his tractor into a wall; he wanted Haroon to pay for the tractor's damage. They behaved angrily and violently, each blaming the other, and the villagers feared there might be bloodshed.

The Decision

Haji Usman first listened to both sides in turn — he instructed Salman to stay quiet while Haroon spoke, then asked Salman to explain his side. He concluded that both deserved some return from each other: Haroon would provide money immediately for the repair of Salman's tractor (Salman needed it repaired urgently), and next year Salman would help Haroon to plough his fields, making up for the damage to the crops. The decision was completely fair; both men shook hands, apologized to each other and became friends again.

Theme

Quarrelling is always harmful, whereas blessed are those who are peacemakers; a wise and impartial conciliator can settle disputes justly by listening to both sides.

Word Meanings

  • piety — deep devotion to religion. quarrel — a fight; an angry argument.
  • accidentally — by accident; without intention. destroyed — ended the existence of something by damaging it.
  • bloodshed — the killing or wounding of people. instructed — directed or ordered.
  • plough — to turn over the soil with a plough. portion — a part of something.
  • wage — a fixed regular payment for work. suddenly — quickly and unexpectedly.
  • smashed — broken violently into pieces; crashed. repaired — fixed; mended.
  • urgently — needing immediate action. immediately — at once; without delay. apologized — said sorry.

options: Haji Usman listened to both sides in turn, and both men owed each other something

mcqs.why: Theme: quarrelling is always harmful, whereas blessed are those who are peacemakers; a wise, impartial conciliator settles disputes by listening to both sides.

lessons.title: Story Skills: Story Elements, Plot and Cause–Effect
lessons.notes_html:
Story Elements of 'Settling the Quarrel'

  • Setting: a little village near Faisalabad; outside the masjid and in the fields.
  • Characters: Haji Usman (wise conciliator), Haroon (farmer), Salman (tractor driver), the villagers.
  • Problem/Conflict: the quarrel over destroyed crops and the damaged tractor.
  • Events: the fight; the villagers' request; Haji Usman listens to Haroon, then to Salman.
  • Resolution: the balanced decision; both men accept, apologize and become friends.
  • Plot: simple, clear and well developed — a beginning (the quarrel), a middle (both sides heard) and a satisfying end (reconciliation). A part that can be improved: showing Salman's feelings and the villagers' reaction in more detail before the decision, to build suspense — 'The crowd held its breath. Salman's hands trembled as he thought of his damaged tractor — his only source of income. Haroon's eyes were wet as he looked at his ruined crops.'

Cause and Effect in the Poem 'Anger'

A cause is the reason why something happened; an effect is the result — what happened. Signal words: because, so, since, as a result, if...then, therefore, due to.

  • Causes of anger: Jason pushed the narrator into the wall; Sophie said he wasn't very tall; Adam called him a very rude name.
  • Effects of anger: a face red and hot; his heart beats a lot; his breathing becomes shallow and fast; he feels a sickness he hopes won't last. Anger prepares the body to fight or to flee; if he is not careful, he could do something rash and then feel very low. So he plans to calm down by counting to ten, running, or breathing slow and deep.

options: simple, clear and well developed, with a beginning, a middle and a satisfying end
mcqs.why: The plot analysis says the plot has a beginning (the quarrel), a middle (both sides heard) and a satisfying end (reconciliation).

options: show Salman's feelings and the villagers' reaction in more detail before the decision, to build suspense
mcqs.why: The model improvement adds suspense before the decision: the crowd holds its breath, Salman's hands tremble, Haroon's eyes are wet.

options: the reason why something happened — the result, what happened

mcqs.why: The cause–effect answer says anger prepares the body to fight or to flee; if not careful, a person may act rashly and feel low afterwards.

lessons.title: Vocabulary and Grammar: Prepositions, Gerunds and Participles, Direct and Indirect Speech
lessons.notes_html:
Compound Prepositions

A compound preposition contains two or more prepositional words: The students are standing in front of the school. Salman, along with Haroon, thanked Haji Usman. Instead of fighting, they should settle the matter peacefully. There is a flag at the top of the building. According to Haji Usman, both men deserved some return from each other.

Prepositional Phrases

A prepositional phrase always starts with a preposition and functions as an adjective phrase or adverb phrase; it has a noun or pronoun as the object of the preposition. From the story: 'in a little village', 'near Faisalabad', 'outside the masjid', 'in the distance', 'through Haroon's fields', 'into a wall'.

Gerunds and Participles

Gerunds (verb + -ing used as a noun): Writing helps me to express my idea. (subject) Sana is good at playing tennis. (object of preposition) Smoking is injurious to health. Eating vegetables and fruits is good for health. Mountaineering is my favourite sport.

Participles (verb + -ing acting as verb/adjective): This is a thrilling story. (adjective) That essay is very boring. (adjective) While watching TV, I heard the knock at the gate. Own sentences: Fishing is my hobby. (gerund) / The man fishing in the river caught a big fish. (participle) Playing cricket keeps us fit. (gerund) / The children playing in the park are my friends. (participle) Teaching is a noble profession. (gerund) / The teacher teaching English is very kind. (participle)

Direct and Indirect Speech — Rules

Simple present changes to simple past; present continuous to past continuous; present perfect to past perfect; can–could, may–might, will–would, shall–should; now–then, here–there, ago–before, today–that day, tomorrow–the next day, yesterday–the day before, last night–the night before; this–that, these–those.

  • Sarwat said, 'I do not like going out much.' → Sarwat said that she did not like going out much.
  • He said, 'They never arrive on time.' → He said that they never arrived on time.
  • They said to us, 'We often visit our friends in Kashmir.' → They told us that they often visited their friends in Kashmir.
  • Afshan said, 'We are not going to the library.' → Afshan said that they were not going to the library.
  • My brother said to me, 'I did not go out at the weekend.' → My brother told me that he had not gone out at the weekend.
  • He said, 'I am driving a car.' → He said that he was driving a car.
  • They said, 'Our work has been finished.' → They said that their work had been finished.
  • He said, 'I have been sick all week.' → He said that he had been sick all week.

lessons.title: Speaking and Writing: Dialogue, Story on 'Anger' and Incident Narration
lessons.notes_html:
Completed Dialogue — Teacher and Students (Model)

Teacher: Do you know that quarrelling or fighting is a bad thing? Students: Yes, teacher. In a quarrel people use harsh talk and bitter words, and sometimes a person acts rashly and later feels sorry. Teacher: Have you ever settled a quarrel of somebody? Students: Yes, teacher. Two of our class fellows quarrelled yesterday. One had talked insolently, but when he realized his mistake, he said sorry, and his apology was accepted. We learnt that we should be careful before accusing anyone. Teacher: We should promote peace and live in harmony.

Story on 'Anger' — 'The Day I Controlled My Anger' (Model)

Mind map: Name: Bilal. Description: a class 8 student, quick-tempered but kind. Friends: Ahmed and Usman. Enemies: none — only his anger. What friends did: calmed him and advised him. What anger did: made him quarrel over a small matter.

Story: One day at school, Bilal's class fellow Danish pushed him in the corridor and called him a rude name. Bilal's face became red and hot, his heart beat fast, and he was ready to fight. He remembered the poem 'Anger' and counted to ten. He breathed slow and deep and walked away instead of giving Danish a bash. Later, Danish came to him, said sorry for his harsh talk, and his apology was accepted. Bilal felt proud: he had not hurt anyone, any property, or himself. From that day, whenever he is angry, he counts to ten — and his anger never lasts.

Incident Narration (Model)

'Last month, my two friends, Ali and Hassan, quarrelled in the classroom. Hassan had accidentally torn Ali's notebook while taking out his books, and Ali blamed him for doing it on purpose. Both used bitter words and were about to fight. I stood between them and asked them to stay quiet. First I listened to Ali, then to Hassan, just as Haji Usman had listened to Haroon and Salman. I told Ali that the notebook was torn by accident, and told Hassan to apologize and help repair it with tape. Hassan said sorry, Ali accepted his apology, and they shook hands. Our teacher praised me and said, "Blessed are those who are peacemakers."'

mcqs.why: The students answer: 'In a quarrel people use harsh talk and bitter words, and sometimes a person acts rashly and later feels sorry.'

options: He came to Bilal, said sorry for his harsh talk, and his apology was accepted

mcqs.why: The butterfly organiser lists: Enemies — none, only his anger; friends Ahmed and Usman calmed and advised him.

lessons.title: Oral and Reading Review: Poem, Review Questions and the Reading Passage
lessons.notes_html:
Poem 'Taking A Tour in Hills' by Hifsa Ambreen — Summary

The poet describes a tour in the hills with her family. The earth was far below and she felt high, breathing fresh air near the sky. Wondering, happy and gay, she went along singing and dancing. The hills were high, frosty and green — an enchanting beauty she had never seen before. At night, outside the hotel room, the star-like lights of the houses up and down the hills presented an amazingly heavenly sight. Brother and sister, mom and dad — everyone around was very glad.

Antonyms: high — low; near — far; happy — sad; beauty — ugliness; night — day; glad — sad/sorry.

Review Questions — Answers

  • Hazrat Umar (RA): Title 'Faruq'. Traits: just and impartial — high and low, rich and poor equal before law; kind and sympathetic to the poor, visiting them in disguise at night; a great administrator and reformer; brave, strong-willed and God-fearing. Reforms: a model system of administration; administrative courts; reforms of army, police force and tax system; protection of non-Muslims' worship places and property.
  • Sports and character: Sports make a person strong-willed and disciplined; they teach honesty, teamwork, fair play, respect, integrity and goodwill toward opponents, and help us face mental pressure.
  • The seasons: Spring — lilacs bloom. Autumn — the maple turns red. Summer — crowned with sunshine. Winter — snow and icicle spears; each season comes with its joys, pleasures and fears.
  • The quarrel: Haroon fought because Salman's tractor had destroyed a large portion of his crops and he wanted payment. Salman drove into the fields because Haroon's sheep suddenly ran onto the road; to avoid hitting them he steered into the fields and smashed his tractor into a wall.

Passage on Reading — Answers

  • Reading enriches our vocabulary because even a 'boring' text can teach us new words; a larger vocabulary helps us express ourselves better.
  • Reading provides knowledge, and knowledge is power; by reading we learn new words and ideas, so reading makes us a more powerful and better speaker. We should read everything we can at school, whether we find it interesting or not.
  • Reading changes the way we understand the world: it gives us a broader perspective, we learn how people live in faraway places and learn about cultures different from our own. Reading is also good for our state of mind — it has a calming effect, lowers stress and helps us relax; it is a positive escape from our troubles.
  • Suitable title: 'Reading Is Power' (or 'The Benefits of Reading').

The Passage Rewritten with Modal Verbs (Model)

'Reading stimulates your mind. It provides knowledge, and knowledge is power. Therefore, reading will make you a more powerful person. You may learn to do new things by reading. You should read everything that you get at school, whether you find it interesting or not, because reading enriches your vocabulary. Even a boring text might teach you new words, and a larger vocabulary would help you express yourself better. Reading must change the way you understand the world and shall give you a broader perspective on things.'

mcqs.why: The passage answer states that even a boring text can teach new words; a larger vocabulary helps us express ourselves better.

mcqs.q: According to the passage, knowledge is ______.
mcqs.why: Reading provides knowledge, and knowledge is power; by reading we learn new words and ideas and become better speakers.

options: It takes us on free tours

mcqs.why: Reading changes the way we understand the world — a broader perspective, faraway lives and cultures different from our own.

options: it has a calming effect, lowers stress and helps us relax
it makes us sleepy in class
it stops all our troubles forever
mcqs.why: The passage calls reading a positive escape from our troubles: calming, lowering stress and helping us relax.

mcqs.why: The suggested titles are 'Reading Is Power' or 'The Benefits of Reading'.
